entries.08d467da080fc123b326674ad2ebfea9a64d0103: <div sID="gen32294" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="2Thess.2" sID="2Thess.2"/> <div eID="gen32294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32295" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32296" type="x-p"/> The apostle is very careful to hinder the spreading of an error into which some among them had fallen concerning the coming of Christ, as being very near, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1-2Thess.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. Then he proceeds to confute the error he cautioned them against, by telling them of two great events that were antecedent to the coming of Christ—a general apostasy, and the revelation of antichrist, concerning whom the apostle tells them many remarkable things, about his name, his character, his rise, his fall, his reign, and the sin and ruin of his subjects, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4-2Thess.2.12">ver. 4-12</reference>. He then comforts them against the terror of this apostasy, and exhorts them to stedfastness, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13-2Thess.2.15">ver. 13-15</reference>. And concludes with a prayer for them, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.16-2Thess.2.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>.
entries.c59abf6e40671c72ebbe497b02dd045c7cb64d88: <div eID="gen32296" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32295" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against False Alarm. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 52.)</title> <div sID="gen32297" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and <hi type="italic">by</hi> our gathering together unto him, <hi type="super">2</hi> That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand. <hi type="super">3</hi> Let no man deceive you by any means— <div eID="gen32297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32298" type="x-p"/> From these words it appears that some among the Thessalonians had mistaken the apostle's meaning, in what he had written in his former epistle about the coming of Christ, by thinking that it was near at hand,—that Christ was just ready to appear and come to judgment. Or, it may be, some among them pretended that they had the knowledge of this by particular revelation from the Spirit, or from some words they had heard from the apostle, when he was with them, or some letter he had written or they pretended he had written to them or some other person: and hereupon the apostle is careful to rectify this mistake, and to prevent the spreading of this error. Observe, If errors and mistakes arise among Christians, we should take the first opportunity to rectify them, and hinder the spreading thereof; and good men will be especially careful to suppress errors that may arise from a mistake of their words and actions, though that which was spoken or done was ever so innocent or well. We have a subtle adversary, who watches all opportunities to do mischief, and will sometimes promote errors even by means of the words of scripture. Observe, <div eID="gen32298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32299" type="x-p"/> I. How very earnest and solicitous this apostle was to prevent mistakes: <hi type="italic">We beseech you, brethren,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">v. 1</reference>. He entreats them as brethren who might have charged them as a father charges his children: he shows great kindness and condescension, and insinuates himself into their affections. And this is the best way to deal with men when we would preserve or recover them from errors, to deal gently and affectionately with them: rough and rigorous treatment will but exasperate their spirits, and prejudice them against the reasons we may offer. He obtests and even conjures them in the most solemn manner: <hi type="italic">By the coming of Christ,</hi> &c. The words are in the form of an oath; and his meaning is that if they believed Christ would come, and if they desired he would come, and rejoiced in the hope of his coming, they should be careful to avoid the error, and the evil consequences of it, against which he was now cautioning them. From this form of obtestation used by the apostle, we may observe, <div eID="gen32299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32300" type="x-p"/> 1. It is most certain that the Lord Jesus Christ will come to judge the world, that he will come in all the pomp and power of the upper world in the last day, to execute judgment upon all. Whatever uncertainty we are at, or whatever mistakes may arise about the time of his coming, his coming itself is certain. This has been the faith and hope of all Christians in all ages of the church; nay, it was the faith and hope of the Old-Testament saints, ever since Enoch the seventh from Adam, who said, <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord cometh,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Jude.1.14">Jude 14</reference>. <div eID="gen32300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32301" type="x-p"/> 2. At the second coming of Christ all the saints will be gathered together to him; and this mention of the gathering of the saints together unto Christ at his coming shows that the apostle speaks of Christ's coming to judgment day, and not of his coming to destroy Jerusalem. He speaks of a proper, and not a metaphorical advent: and, as it will be part of Christ's honour in that day, so it will be the completing of the happiness of his saints. (1.) That they all shall be gathered together. There will then be a general meeting of all the saints, and none but saints; all the Old-Testament saints, who got acquaintance with Christ by the dark shadows of the law, and saw this day at a distance; and all the New-Testament saints, to whom life and immortality were brought to light by the gospel; they will all be gathered together. There will then come from the four winds of heaven all that are, or ever were, or ever shall be, from the beginning to the end of time. All shall be gathered together. (2.) That they shall be gathered <hi type="italic">together to Christ.</hi> He will be the great centre of their unity. They shall be gathered together to him, to be attendants on him, to be assessors with him, to be presented by him to the Father, to be with him for ever, and altogether happy in his presence to all eternity. (3.) The doctrine of Christ's coming and our gathering together to him is of a great moment and importance to Christians; otherwise it would not be the proper matter of the apostle's obtestation. We ought therefore not only to believe these things, but highly to account of them also, and look upon them as things we are greatly concerned in and should be much affected with. <div eID="gen32301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32302" type="x-p"/> II. The thing itself against which the apostle cautions the Thessalonians is that they should not be deceived about the time of Christ's coming, and so <hi type="italic">be shaken in mind, or be troubled.</hi> Note, Errors in the mind tend greatly to weaken our faith, and cause us trouble; and such as are weak in faith and of troubled minds are oftentimes apt to be deceived, and fall a prey to seducers. 1. The apostle would not have them be deceived: <hi type="italic">Let no man deceive you by any means,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">v. 3</reference>. There are many who lie in wait to deceive, and they have many ways of deceiving; we have reason therefore to be cautious and stand upon our guard. Some deceivers will pretend new revelations, others misinterpret scripture, and others will be guilty of gross forgeries; divers means and artifices of deceit men will use; but we must be careful that no man deceive us by any means. The particular matter in which the apostle cautions them not to be deceived is about the near approach of Christ's coming, as if it was to have been in the apostle's days; and harmless as this error might seem to many, yet, because it was indeed an error, it would have proved of bad consequences to many persons. Therefore, 2. He gives them warning, and would not have them be soon shaken in mind, nor be troubled. (1.) He would not have their faith weakened. We should firmly believe the second coming of Christ, and be settled and established in the faith of this; but there was danger lest the Thessalonians, if they apprehended the coming of Christ was just at hand, upon finding that they, or others whom they too much regarded, were mistaken as to the time, should thereupon question the truth or certainty of the thing itself; whereas they ought not to waver in their minds as to this great thing, which is the faith and hope of all the saints. False doctrines are like winds, that toss the water to and fro, and they are apt to unsettle the minds of men, who are sometimes as unstable as water. Then, (2.) He would not have their comforts lessened, that they should not be troubled nor affrighted with false alarms. It is probable that the coming of Christ was represented in so much terror as to trouble many serious Christians among them, though in itself it should be matter of the believer's hope and joy; or else many might be troubled with the thought how surprising this day would be, or with the fear of their unpreparedness, or upon the reflection on their mistake about the time of Christ's coming: we should always watch and pray, but must not be discouraged nor uncomfortable at the thought of Christ's coming.
entries.6ddf134718d38e1c749d1e365a2b6ab570d66651: <div eID="gen32312" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostasy Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 52.)</title> <div sID="gen32313" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth: <hi type="super">14</hi> Whereunto he called you by our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. <hi type="super">15</hi> Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle. <div eID="gen32313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32314" type="x-p"/> Here observe, I. The consolation the Thessalonians might take against the terrors of this apostasy, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13-2Thess.2.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. For they were chosen to salvation, and called to the obtaining of glory. Note, When we hear of the apostasy of many, it is matter of great comfort and joy that there is a remnant according to the election of grace which does and shall persevere; and especially we should rejoice if we have reason to hope that we are of that number. The apostle reckoned himself bound in duty to be thankful to God on this account: <hi type="italic">We are bound to give thanks to God always for you.</hi> He had often given thanks on their behalf, and he is still abounding in thanksgiving for them; and there was good reason, because they were beloved by the Lord, as appeared in this matter—their security from apostatizing. This preservation of the saints is owing, <div eID="gen32314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32315" type="x-p"/> 1. To the stability of the election of grace, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">v. 13</reference>. Therefore were they beloved of the Lord, because God had chosen them from the beginning. He had loved them with an everlasting love. Concerning this election of God we may observe, (1.) The eternal date of it—it is from the beginning; not the beginning of the gospel, but the beginning of the world, before the foundation of the world, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Eph. i. 4</reference>. Then, (2.) The end to which they were chosen—salvation, complete and eternal salvation from sin and misery, and the full fruition of all good. (3.) The means in order to obtaining this end—<hi type="italic">sanctification of the spirit and belief of the truth.</hi> The decree of election therefore connects the end and the means, and these must not be separated. We are not the elected of God because we were holy, but that we might be holy. Being chosen of God, we must not live as we list; but, if we are chosen to salvation as the end, we must be prepared for it by sanctification as the necessary means to obtain that end, which sanctification is by the operation of the Holy Spirit as the author and by faith on our part. There must be the belief of the truth, without which there can be by true sanctification, nor perseverance in grace, nor obtaining of salvation. Faith and holiness must be joined together, as well as holiness and happiness; therefore our Saviour prayed for Peter that his faith might not fail (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>), and for his disciples (<reference osisRef="John.17.17">John xvii. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">Sanctify them by thy truth; thy word is truth.</hi> <div eID="gen32315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32316" type="x-p"/> 2. To the efficacy of the gospel call, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.14">v. 14</reference>. As they were chosen to salvation, so they were called thereunto by the gospel. Whom he did predestinate those he also called, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Rom. viii. 30</reference>. The outward call of God is by the gospel; and this is rendered effectual by the inward operation of the Spirit. Note, Wherever the gospel comes it calls and invites men to the obtaining of glory; it is a call to honour and happiness, even the <hi type="italic">glory of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> the glory he has purchased, and the glory he is possessed of, to be communicated unto those who believe in him and obey his gospel; such shall be with Christ, to behold his glory, and they shall be glorified with Christ and partake of his glory. Hereupon there follows, <div eID="gen32316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32317" type="x-p"/> II. An exhortation to stedfastness and perseverance: <hi type="italic">Therefore, brethren, stand fast,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Observe, He does not say, "You are chosen to salvation, and therefore you may be careless and secure;" but <hi type="italic">therefore stand fast.</hi> God's grace in our election and vocation is so far from superseding our diligent care and endeavour that it should quicken and engage us to the greatest resolution and diligence. So the apostle John having told those to whom he wrote that they had received the anointing which should abide in them, and that they should abide in him (in Christ), subjoins this exhortation, <hi type="italic">Now abide in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.27-1John.2.28">1 John ii. 27, 28</reference>. The Thessalonians are exhorted to stedfastness in their Christian profession, to <hi type="italic">hold fast the traditions which they had been taught,</hi> or the doctrine of the gospel, which had been delivered by the apostle, by word or epistle. As yet the canon of scripture was not complete, and therefore some things were delivered by the apostles in their preaching, under the guidance of the infallible Spirit, which Christians were bound to observe as coming from God; other things were afterwards by them committed to writing, as the apostle had written a former epistle to these Thessalonians; and these epistles were written as the writers were moved by the Holy Ghost. Note, There is no argument hence for regarding oral traditions in our days, now that the canon of scripture is complete, as of equal authority with the sacred writings. Such doctrines and duties as were taught by the inspired apostles we must stedfastly adhere to; but we have no certain evidence of any thing delivered by them more than what we find contained in the holy scriptures.
entries.d5b85bf64591edc958361030e1b6c0a4e9f28bf7: <div eID="gen32317" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostolic Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 52.)</title> <div sID="gen32318" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, which hath loved us, and hath given <hi type="italic">us</hi> everlasting consolation and good hope through grace, <hi type="super">17</hi> Comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work. <div eID="gen32318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32319" type="x-p"/> In these words we have the apostle's earnest prayer for them, in which observe, <div eID="gen32319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32320" type="x-p"/> I. To whom he prays: <hi type="italic">Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father.</hi> We may and should direct our prayers, not only to God the Father, through the mediation of our Lord Jesus Christ, but also <hi type="italic">to our Lord Jesus Christ himself;</hi> and should pray in his name unto God, not only as his Father but as our Father in and through him. <div eID="gen32320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32321" type="x-p"/> II. From what he takes encouragement in his prayer—from the consideration of what God had already done for him and them: <hi type="italic">Who hath loved us, and given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.16">v. 16</reference>. Here observe, 1. The love of God is the spring and fountain of all the good we have or hope for; our election, vocation, justification, and salvation, are all owing to the love of God in Christ Jesus. 2. From this fountain in particular all our consolation flows. And the consolation of the saints is an everlasting consolation. The comforts of the saints are not dying things; they shall not die with them. The spiritual consolations God gives none shall deprive them of; and God will not take them away: because he love them with an everlasting love, therefore they shall have everlasting consolation. 3. Their consolation is founded on the hope of eternal life. They rejoice in hope of the glory of God, and are not only patient, but joyful, in tribulations; and there is good reason for these strong consolations, because the saints have good hope: their hope is grounded on the love of God, the promise of God, and the experience they have had of the power, the goodness, and the faithfulness of God, and it is good hope through grace; the free grace and mercy of God are what they hope for, and what their hopes are founded on, and not on any worth or merit of their own. <div eID="gen32321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32322" type="x-p"/> III. What it is that he asks of God for them—that <hi type="italic">he would comfort their hearts, and establish them in every good word and work,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.17">v. 17</reference>. God had given them consolations, and he prayed that they might have more abundant consolation. There was good hope, through grace, that they would be preserved, and he prayed that they might be established: it is observable how comfort and establishment are here joined together. Note therefore, 1. Comfort is a means of establishment; for the more pleasure we take in the word, and work, and ways of God, the more likely we shall be to persevere therein. And, 2. Our establishment in the ways of God is a likely means in order to comfort; whereas, if we are wavering in faith, and of a doubtful mind, or if we are halting and faltering in our duty, no wonder if we are strangers to the pleasures and joys of religion. What is it that lies at the bottom of all our uneasiness, but our unsteadiness in religion? We must be established in every good word and work, in the word of truth and the work of righteousness: Christ must be honoured by our good works and good words; and those who are sincere will endeavour to do both, and in so doing they may hope for comfort and establishment, till at length their holiness and happiness be completed.  <chapter eID="2Thess.2"/> <div eID="gen32322" type="x-p"/>

entries.b19b15d311f476bf2053f7b4cd2969a6c1eb6b5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18021"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen36915" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1-2Thess.2.17">2Th 2:1-17</reference>. Correction of Their Error as to Christ's Immediate Coming. The Apostasy that Must Precede It. Exhortation to Steadfastness, Introduced with Thanksgiving for Their Election by God.<div eID="gen36915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18021"/><hi type="bold">1. Now--</hi>rather, "But"; marking the transition from his prayers for them to entreaties to them.<div eID="gen36916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we beseech you--</hi>or "entreat you." He uses affectionate entreaty, rather than stern reproof, to win them over to the right view.<div eID="gen36917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>rather, "with respect to"; as the Greek for "of" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">2Co 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our gathering together unto him--</hi>the consummating or final gathering together of the saints to Him at His coming, as announced, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">Mt 24:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">1Th 4:17</reference>. The Greek noun is nowhere else found except in <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>, said of the assembling together of believers for congregational worship. Our instinctive fears of the judgment are dispelled by the thought of being gathered together UNTO Him ("even as the hen gathereth her chickens under her wings"), which ensures our safety. <div eID="gen36919" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6f5bdb74db473c12cce7baf267f509a3ea0616b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18022"/><div sID="gen36920" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18022"/><hi type="bold">2. soon--</hi>on trifling grounds, without due consideration.<div eID="gen36920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shaken--</hi>literally, "tossed" as ships tossed by an agitated sea. Compare for the same image, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>.<div eID="gen36921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in mind--</hi>rather as the Greek, "from your mind," that is, from your mental steadfastness on the subject.<div eID="gen36922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">troubled--</hi>This verb applies to emotional agitation; as "shaken" to intellectual.<div eID="gen36923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by spirit--</hi>by a person professing to have the spirit of prophecy (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.8-1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1-1John.4.3">1Jo 4:1-3</reference>). The Thessalonians had been warned (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.20">1Th 5:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">21</reference>) to "prove" such professed prophesyings, and to "hold fast (only) that which is good."<div eID="gen36924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by word--</hi>of mouth (compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.5">2Th 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>); some word or saying alleged to be that of Paul, orally communicated. If oral tradition was liable to such perversion in the apostolic age (compare a similar instance, <reference osisRef="John.21.23">Joh 21:23</reference>), how much more in our age!<div eID="gen36925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by letter as from us--</hi>purporting to be from us, whereas it is a forgery. Hence he gives a test by which to know his genuine letters (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.17">2Th 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "day of the Lord."<div eID="gen36927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is at hand--</hi>rather, "is immediately imminent," literally, "is present"; "is instantly coming." Christ and His apostles always taught that the day of the Lord's coming is at hand; and it is not likely that Paul would imply anything contrary here; what he denies is, that it is so immediately imminent, instant, or present, as to justify the neglect of everyday worldly duties. Chrysostom, and after him Alford, translates, "is (already) present" (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>), a kindred error. But in <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1">2Ti 3:1</reference>, the same Greek verb is translated "come." Wahl supports this view. The Greek is usually used of actual presence; but is quite susceptible of the translation, "is all but present." <div eID="gen36928" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0dbfe49127644da8b8a74a1a71c38d7961378d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18023"/><div sID="gen36929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18023"/><hi type="bold">3. by any means--</hi>Greek, "in any manner." Christ, in <reference osisRef="Matt.24.4">Mt 24:4</reference>, gives the same warning in connection with the same event. He had indicated three ways (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>) in which they might be deceived (compare other ways, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">Mt 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">24</reference>).<div eID="gen36929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a falling away--</hi>rather as the Greek, "the falling away," or "apostasy," namely, the one of which "I told you" before (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.5">2Th 2:5</reference>), "when I was yet with you," and of which the Lord gave some intimation (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.10-Matt.24.12">Mt 24:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.43">Joh 5:43</reference>).<div eID="gen36930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that man of sin be revealed--</hi>The Greek order is, "And there have been revealed the man of sin." As Christ was first in mystery, and afterwards revealed (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), so Antichrist (the term used <reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1Jo 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">4:3</reference>) is first in mystery, and afterwards shall be developed and revealed (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7-2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:7-9</reference>). As righteousness found its embodiment in Christ, "the Lord our righteousness," so "sin" shall have its embodiment in "the man of sin." The hindering power meanwhile restrains its manifestation; when that shall be removed, then this manifestation shall take place. The articles, "the apostasy," and "the man of sin," may also refer to their being well known as foretold in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.8">Da 7:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">25</reference>, "the little horn speaking great words against the Most High, and thinking to change times and laws"; and <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>, the wilful king who "shall exalt and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvellous things against the God of gods; neither shall he regard any god."<div eID="gen36931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the son of perdition--</hi>a title applied besides to Judas (the traitor, <reference osisRef="John.17.12">Joh 17:12</reference>), and to none else. Antichrist (the second "beast" coming up out of the earth); therefore he shall at first be "like a lamb, while he speaks as a dragon" (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.11">Re 13:11</reference>); "coming in peaceably and by flatteries," "working deceitfully," but "his heart shall be against the holy covenant" (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.21">Da 11:21</reference>, 23, 28, 30). Seeds of "the falling away" soon appear (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:1-3</reference>), but the full development and concentration of these anti-Christian elements in one person are still to appear. Contrast the King of Zion's coming as Jesus: (1) righteous or just; (2) having salvation; (3) lowly; whereas Antichrist is: (1) "the man of (the embodiment of) sin; (2) the son of perdition; (3) exalting himself above all that is worshipped. He is the son of perdition, as consigning many to it, and finally doomed to it himself (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.8">Re 17:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.11">11</reference>). "He whose essence and inheritance is perdition" [Alford]. As "the kingdom of heaven" is first brought before us in the abstract, then in the concrete, the King, the Lord Jesus; so here, first we have (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7">2Th 2:7</reference>) "the mystery of iniquity," then "the iniquitous one" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>). Doubtless "the apostasy" of Romanism (the abstract) is one of the greatest instances of the working of the mystery of iniquity, and its blasphemous claims for the Pope (the concrete) are forerunners of the final concentration of blasphemy in the man of sin, who shall not merely, as the Pope, usurp God's honor as vicegerent of God, but oppose God openly at last. <div eID="gen36932" type="x-p"/>
entries.faff8680a629fff0b9fdb9acaa590bd9e7d33f0d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18024"/><div sID="gen36933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18024"/>4. <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">37</reference> is here referred to. The words used there as to Antiochus Epiphanes, Paul implies, shall even be more applicable to the man of sin, who is the New Testament actual Antichrist, as Antiochus was the Old Testament typical Antichrist. The previous world kingdoms had each one extraordinary person as its representative head and embodiment (thus Babylon had Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Da 2:38</reference>, end; Medo-Persia had Cyrus; Greece had Alexander, and Antiochus Epiphanes, the forerunner of Antichrist); so the fourth and last world kingdom, under which we now live, shall have one final head, the concentrated embodiment of all the sin and lawless iniquity which have been in pagan and papal Rome. Rome's final phase will probably be an unholy alliance between idolatrous superstition and godless infidelity.<div eID="gen36933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Who opposeth and exalteth himself--</hi>There is but one Greek article to both participles, implying that the reason why he opposeth himself is in order that he may exalt himself above, &c. Alford takes the former clause absolutely, "He that withstands (Christ)," that is, Antichrist (<reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1Jo 2:18</reference>). As at the conclusion of the Old Testament period, Israel apostate allied itself with the heathen world power against Jesus and His apostles (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.12">Lu 23:12</reference>; and at Thessalonica, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.5-Acts.17.9">Ac 17:5-9</reference>), and was in righteous retribution punished by the instrumentality of the world power itself (Jerusalem being destroyed by Rome), <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">27</reference>; so the degenerate Church (become an "harlot"), allying itself with the godless world power (the "beast" of Revelation) against vital religion (that is, the harlot sitting on the beast), shall be judged by that world power which shall be finally embodied in Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">Zec 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.16">Re 17:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.17">17</reference>). In this early Epistle, the apostate Jewish Church as the harlot, and pagan Rome as the beast, form the historical background on which Paul draws his prophetic sketch of the apostasy. In the Pastoral Epistles, which were later, this prophecy appears in connection with Gnosticism, which had at that time infected the Church. The harlot (the apostate Church) is first to be judged by the beast (the world power) and its kings (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.16">Re 17:16</reference>); and afterwards the beasts and their allies (with the personal Antichrist at their head, who seems to rise after the judgment on the harlot, or apostate Church) shall be judged by the coming of Jesus Himself (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">Re 19:20</reference>). Anti-Christian tendencies produce different Antichrists: these separate Antichrists shall hereafter find their consummation in an individual exceeding them all in the intensity of his evil character [Auberlen]. But judgment soon overtakes him. He is necessarily a child of death, immediately after his ascent as the beast out of the bottomless pit going into perdition (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.8">Re 17:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.11">11</reference>). Idolatry of self, spiritual pride, and rebellion against God, are his characteristics; as Christ-worship, humility, and dependence on God, characterize Christianity. He not merely assumes Christ's character (as the "false Christs," <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference>), but "opposes" Christ. The Greek implies one situated on an opposite side (compare <reference osisRef="1John.2.22">1Jo 2:22</reference>; 2Jo 7). One who, on the destruction of every religion, shall seek to establish his own throne, and for God's great truth, "God is man," to substitute his own lie, "Man is God" [Trench].<div eID="gen36934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">above all that is called God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.5">1Co 8:5</reference>). The Pope (for instance, Clement VI) has even commanded the angels to admit into Paradise, without the alleged pains of purgatory, certain souls. But still this is only a foreshadowing of the Antichrist, who will not, as the Pope, act in God's name, but against God.<div eID="gen36935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or that is worshipped--</hi>Rome here again gives a presage of Antichrist. The Greek is Sebasma; and Sebastus is the Greek for Augustus, who was worshipped as the secular ruler and divine vicegerent. The papacy has risen on the overthrow of Cæsar's power. Antichrist shall exalt himself above every object of worship, whether on earth as the Cæsar, or in heaven as God. The various prefigurations of Antichrist, Mohammed, Rome, Napoleon, and modern infidel secularism, contain only some, not all, his characteristics. It is the union of all in some one person that shall form the full Antichrist, as the union in one Person, Jesus, of all the types and prophecies constituted the full Christ [Olshausen].<div eID="gen36936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the temple of God ... that he is God--</hi>"He will reign a time, times, and half a time" (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>), that is, three and a half years, and will sit in the temple at Jerusalem: then the Lord shall come from heaven and cast him into the take of fire and shall bring to the saints the times of their reigning, the seventh day of hallowed rest, and give to Abraham the promised inheritance" [Irenæus, Against Heresies, 30.4].<div eID="gen36937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">showing himself--</hi>with blasphemous and arrogant DISPLAY (compare a type, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.21-Acts.12.23">Ac 12:21-23</reference>). The earliest Fathers unanimously looked for a personal Antichrist. Two objections exist to Romanism being regarded the Antichrist, though probably Romanism will leave its culmination in him: (1) So far is Romanism from opposing all that is called God, that adoration of gods and lords many (the Virgin Mary and saints) is a leading feature in it; (2) the papacy has existed for more than twelve centuries, and yet Christ is not come, whereas the prophecy regards the final Antichrist as short-lived, and soon going to perdition through the coming of Christ (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.8">Re 17:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.11">11</reference>). Gregory the Great declared against the patriarch of Constantinople, that whosoever should assume the title of "universal bishop" would be "the forerunner of Antichrist." The papacy fulfilled this his undesigned prophecy. The Pope has been called by his followers, "Our Lord God the Pope"; and at his inauguration in St. Peter's, seated in his chair upon the high altar, which is treated as his footstool, he has vividly foreshadowed him who "exalteth himself above all that is called God." An objection fatal to interpreting the temple of God here as the Church (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">6:19</reference>) is, the apostle would never designate the apostate anti-Christian Church "the temple of God." It is likely that, as Messiah was revealed among the Jews at Jerusalem, so Antimessiah shall appear among them when restored to their own land, and after they have rebuilt their temple at Jerusalem. Thus <reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">Da 11:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">45</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">Da 11:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">Da 11:45</reference>), corresponds, "He shall enter the glorious land (Judea), and he shall plant the tabernacles of his palaces between the seas in the glorious holy mountain"; and then (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>) "Michael, the great prince, shall stand up" to deliver God's people. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">27</reference>. Also the king of Assyria, type of Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.12-Isa.14.14">Is 14:12-14</reference>). "Lucifer" (a title of Messiah, assumed by Antichrist, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Re 22:16</reference>); "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God." "I will sit upon the mount of the congregation (that is, God's place of meeting His people of old, the temple), in the sides of the north (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>); I will be like the Most High." <reference osisRef="Rev.11.1">Re 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2</reference>, "The temple of God ... the holy city" (namely, Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.5">Mt 4:5</reference>), compare <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">29</reference>, referring to a period since Christ's ascension, therefore not yet fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.3">Is 2:1-3</reference>; Eze 40:1-44:31; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16-Zech.14.20">Zec 14:16-20</reference>; Mal 3:1). "In the temple of God," implies that it an internal, not an external, enemy which shall assail the Church. Antichrist shall, the first three and a half years of the prophetical week, keep the covenant, then break it and usurp divine honors in the midst of the week. Some think Antichrist will be a Jew. At all events he will, "by flatteries," bring many, not only of the Gentiles, but also of "the tribes" of Israel (so the Greek for "kindreds," <reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Re 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.9">9</reference>), to own him as their long-looked-for Messiah, in the same "city where our Lord was crucified." "Sitteth" here implies his occupying the place of power and majesty in opposition to Him who "sitteth on the right hand of the Majesty on high" (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>), and who shall come to "sit" there where the usurper had sat (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Mt 26:64</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.2">Re 11:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">3, 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.11">11</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.2">Eze 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.6">3, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.10">9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.14">13, 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.16">16</reference>, as to Tyre, the type of Antichrist, characterized by similar blasphemous arrogance. <div eID="gen36938" type="x-p"/>
entries.123d9f73c1e66505fd5d1d00fde6bece8da3e348: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18025"/><div sID="gen36939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18025"/><hi type="bold">5. Remember, &c.--</hi>confuting those who represent Paul as having labored under error as to Christ's immediate coming when writing his first Epistle, and as now correcting that error.<div eID="gen36939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I told you--</hi>more than once, literally, "I was telling," or "used to tell." <div eID="gen36940" type="x-p"/>
entries.74963170fd57b2f3a1dc8e64660edddbb5ad33cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18026"/><div sID="gen36941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18026"/><hi type="bold">6. now ye know--</hi>by my having told you. The power must have been one "known" to the Thessalonians.<div eID="gen36941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what withholdeth--</hi>that which holds him back; "keeps him in check": the power that has restrained the man of sin from his full and final development, is the moral and conservative influence of political states [Olshausen]: the fabric of human polity as a coercive power; as "he who now letteth" refers to those who rule that polity by which the great upbursting of godlessness is kept down [Alford]. The "what withholdeth" refers to the general hindrance; "he who now letteth," to the person in whom that hindrance is summed up. Romanism, as a forerunner of Antichrist, was thus kept in check by the Romanemperor (the then representative of the coercive power) until Constantine, having removed the seat of empire to Constantinople, the Roman bishop by degrees first raised himself to precedency, then to primacy, and then to sole empire above the secular power. The historical fact from which Paul starts in his prediction was probably the emperor Claudius' expulsion of the Jews, the representative of the anti-Christian adversary in Paul's day, from Rome, thus "withholding" them in some degree in their attacks on Christianity; this suggested the principle holding good to the end of time, and about to find its final fulfilment in the removal of the withholding person or authority, whereupon Antichrist in his worst shape shall start up.<div eID="gen36942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he might be--</hi>Greek, "in order that": ye know that which keeps him back, in God's purposes, from being sooner manifested, "in order that he may be revealed in his own time" (that is, the time appointed by God to him as his proper time for being manifested), not sooner (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.11.35">Da 11:35</reference>). The removal of the withholding power will be when the civil polity, derived from the Roman empire, which is to be, in its last form, divided into ten kingdoms (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.11-Rev.17.13">11-13</reference>), shall, with its leading representative head for the time being ("he who now letteth," Greek, "withholdeth," as in <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.6">2Th 2:6</reference>), yield to the prevalent godless "lawlessness" with "the lawless one" as its embodiment. The elect Church and the Spirit cannot well be, as De Burgh suggests, the withholding power meant; for both shall never be wholly "taken out of the way" (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>). However, the testimony of the elect Church, and the Spirit in her, are the great hindrance to the rise of the apostasy; and it is possible that, though the Lord shall have a faithful few even then, yet the full energy of the Spirit in the visible Church, counteracting the energy or "working" of "the mystery of lawlessness" by the testimony of the elect, shall have been so far "taken out of the way," or set aside, as to admit the manifestation of "the lawless one"; and so De Burgh's'S view may be right (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Lu 18:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.3-Rev.11.12">Re 11:3-12</reference>). This was a power of which the Thessalonians might easily "know" through Paul's instruction. <div eID="gen36943" type="x-p"/>
entries.b55564aefc2f7a9cbe42b374ee7c66d658d9bb2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18027"/><div sID="gen36944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18027"/><hi type="bold">7. the mystery of iniquity--</hi>the counterwork to "the mystery of godliness" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>). Anti-Christianity latently working, as distinguished from its final open manifestation. "Mystery" in Scripture means, not what remains always a secret, but that which is for a while hidden, but in due time manifested (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.3.4">Ep 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">5</reference>). Satan will resort to a mode of opposition more conformed to the then imminent "appearing" and "presence" of the Saviour, and will anticipate Him with a last effort to maintain the dominion of the world [De Burgh], just as at His first advent he rushed into open opposition, by taking possession of the bodies of men. "Iniquity," Greek, "lawlessness"; defiant rejection of God's law (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Zech.5.9">Zec 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.5.10">Zec 5:10</reference>). "Wickedness" (translated by the Septuagint by the same Greek, meaning "lawlessness," which Paul employs here), embodied there as a woman, answers to "the mystery of iniquity," here embodied finally in "the man of sin": as the former was ultimately banished for ever from the Holy Land to her own congenial soil, Babylon, so iniquity and the man of sin shall fall before Michael and the Lord Himself, who shall appear as the Deliverer of His people (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.1-Dan.12.3">Da 12:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.3-Zech.14.9">Zec 14:3-9</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.12.43">Mt 12:43</reference>. The Jewish nation dispossessed of the evil spirit, the demon of idolatry being cast out through the Babylonian captivity, receives ultimately a worse form of the evil spirit, Christ-opposing self-righteousness. Also, the Christian Church in course of time taken possession of by the demon of Romish idolatry, then dispossessed of it by the Reformation, then its house "garnished" by hypocrisy, secularity, and rationalism, but "swept empty" of living faith, then finally apostatizing and repossessed by "the man of sin," and outwardly destroyed for a brief time (though even then Christ shall have witnesses for Him among both the Jews, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">Zec 13:9</reference>, and Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>), when Christ shall suddenly come (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.32-Dan.11.45">Da 11:32-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">Lu 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen36944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">already--</hi>(2Jo 9, 10; <reference osisRef="Col.2.18-Col.2.23">Col 2:18-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>); compare "even now already" (<reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1Jo 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">4:3</reference>) as distinguished from "in his own time" of being revealed hereafter. Antiquity, it appears from hence, is not a justification for unscriptural usages or dogmas, since these were "already," even in Paul's time, beginning to spring up: the written word is the only sure test. "Judaism infecting Christianity is the fuel; the mystery of iniquity is the spark." "It is one and the same impurity diffusing itself over many ages" [Bengel].<div eID="gen36945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">only he who now letteth will let--</hi>The italicized words are not in the Greek. Therefore, translate rather, "only (that is, the continuance of the MYSTERY of iniquity-working will be only) until he who now withholdeth (the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.6">2Th 2:6</reference>) be taken out of the way." "Only (waiting, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">He 10:13</reference>) until he," &c. Then it will work no longer in mystery, but in open manifestation. <div eID="gen36946" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1f0a2e2286be23033299c2bcee96b9b197dbf31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18028"/><div sID="gen36947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18028"/>8. Translate, "the lawless one"; the embodiment of all the godless "lawlessness" which has been working in "mystery" for ages (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7">2Th 2:7</reference>): "the man of sin" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2Th 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom the Lord--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts read, "the Lord Jesus." How awful that He whose very name means God-Saviour, should appear as the Destroyer; but the salvation of the Church requires the destruction of her foe. As the reign of Israel in Canaan was ushered in by judgments on the nations for apostasy (for the Canaanites were originally worshippers of the true God: thus Melchisedek, king of Salem, was the "priest of the most high God," <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Ge 14:18</reference>: Ammon and Moab came from righteous Lot), so the Son of David's reign in Zion and over the whole earth, is to be ushered in by judgments on the apostate Christian world.<div eID="gen36948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consume ... and ... destroy--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Dan.7.26">Da 7:26</reference>, "consume and destroy"; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">Da 11:45</reference>. He shall "consume" him by His mere breath (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">30:33</reference>): the sentence of judgment being the sharp sword that goeth out of His mouth (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Re 19:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.21">21</reference>). Antichrist's manifestation and destruction are declared in the same breath; at his greatest height he is nearest his fall, like Herod his type (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.24-Isa.1.27">Is 1:24-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.20-Acts.12.23">Ac 12:20-23</reference>). As the advancing fire, while still at a distance consumes little insects [Chrysostom] by its mere heat, so Christ's mere approach is enough to consume Antichrist. The mere "appearance of the coming" of the Lord of glory is sufficient to show to Antichrist his perfect nothingness. He is seized and "cast alive into the take of fire" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">Re 19:20</reference>). So the world kingdoms, and the kingdom of the beast, give place to that of the Son of man and His saints. The Greek for "destroy" means "abolish" (the same Greek is so translated, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>); that is, cause every vestige of him to disappear. Compare as to Gog attacking Israel and destroyed by Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.1-Ezek.39.29">Eze 38:1-39:29</reference>), so as not to leave a vestige of him.<div eID="gen36949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the brightness of his coming--</hi>Greek, "the manifestation, (or appearance) of His presence": the first outburst of His advent--the first gleam of His presence--is enough to abolish utterly all traces of Antichrist, as darkness disappears before the dawning day. Next, his adherents are "slain with the sword out of His mouth" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.21">Re 19:21</reference>). Bengel's distinction between "the appearance of His coming" and the "coming" itself is not justified by <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">1Ti 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>, where the same Greek for "appearing" (English Version, here "the brightness") plainly refers to the coming itself. The expression, "manifestation (appearing) of His presence," is used in awful contrast to the revelation of the wicked one in the beginning of the verse. <div eID="gen36950" type="x-p"/>
entries.1dafb41e7215b60e6f0a57de280ff3e108cf9504: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18029"/><div sID="gen36951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18029"/><hi type="bold">9. whose coming--</hi>The same Greek as was used for the Lord's coming (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>) or personal "presence."<div eID="gen36951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is--</hi>in its essential character.<div eID="gen36952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after--</hi>according to the working ("energy") of Satan, as opposed to the energy or working of the Holy Spirit in the Church (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>). As Christ is related to God, so is Antichrist to Satan, his visible embodiment and manifestation: Satan works through him. <reference osisRef="Rev.13.2">Re 13:2</reference>, "The dragon gave him (the beast) his power ... seat ... great authority."<div eID="gen36953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lying wonders--</hi>literally, "wonders" or "prodigies of falsehood." His "power, signs, and wonders," all have falsehood for their base, essence, and aim (<reference osisRef="John.8.44">Joh 8:44</reference>), [Alford]. In <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference> Jesus implies that the miracles shall be real, though demoniac, such mysterious effects of the powers of darkness as we read of in the case of the Egyptian sorcerers, not such as Jesus performed in their character, power, or aim; for they are against the revealed Word, and therefore not to be accepted as evidences of truth; nay, on the authority of that sure Word of prophecy (here, and <reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference>), to be known and rejected as wrought in support of falsehood (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.3.5">De 13:1-3, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Ga 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>; Re 13:11-15; 19:20). The same three Greek words occur for miracles of Jesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.22">Ac 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.4">He 2:4</reference>); showing that as the Egyptian magicians imitated Moses (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.8">2Ti 3:1-8</reference>), so Antichrist will try to imitate Christ's works as a "sign," or proof of divinity. <div eID="gen36954" type="x-p"/>
entries.369da836ab7c706417003ce57f3e813970320042: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18030"/><div sID="gen36955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18030"/><hi type="bold">10. deceivableness--</hi>rather as Greek, "deceit of (to promote) unrighteousness" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen36955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions omit "in." Translate, "unto them that are perishing" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2Co 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">4:3</reference>): the victims of him whose very name describes his perishing nature, "the son of perdition"; in contrast to you whom (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>) "God hath from the beginning chosen to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth."<div eID="gen36956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because--</hi>literally, "in requital for"; in just retribution for their having no love for the truth which was within their reach (on account of its putting a check on their bad passions), and for their having "pleasure in unrighteousness" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.18">Ro 1:18</reference>); they are lost because they loved not, but rejected, the truth which would have saved them.<div eID="gen36957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">received not--</hi>Greek, "welcomed not"; admitted it not cordially.<div eID="gen36958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love of the truth--</hi>not merely love of truth, but love of THE truth (and of, Jesus who is the Truth, in opposition to Satan's "lie," <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.42-John.8.44">Joh 8:42-44</reference>), can save (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.21">Ep 4:21</reference>). We are required not merely to assent to, but to love the truth (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.97">Psa 119:97</reference>). The Jews rejected Him who came in His divine Father's name; they will receive Antichrist coming in his own name (<reference osisRef="John.5.43">Joh 5:43</reference>). Their pleasant sin shall prove their terrible scourge. <div eID="gen36959" type="x-p"/>
entries.12fcdb01e258b1a444db358c2402663d8a58e6fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18031"/><div sID="gen36960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18031"/><hi type="bold">11. for this cause--</hi>because "they received not the love of the truth." The best safeguard against error is "the love of the truth."<div eID="gen36960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall send--</hi>Greek, "sends," or "is sending"; the "delusion" is already beginning. God judicially sends hardness of heart on those who have rejected the truth, and gives them up in righteous judgment to Satan's delusions (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">10</reference>; Ro 1:24-26, 28). They first cast off the love of the truth, then God gives them up to Satan's delusions, then they settle down into "believing the lie": an awful climax (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.22">1Ki 22:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.9">Eze 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job 12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">Mt 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong delusion--</hi>Greek, "the powerful working of error," answering to the energizing "working of Satan" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:9</reference>); the same expression as is applied to the Holy Ghost's operation in believers: "powerful" or "effectual (energizing) working" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen36962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believe a lie--</hi>rather, "the lie" which Antichrist tells them, appealing to his miracles as proofs of it ... (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.9">2Th 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen36963" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8427172cfa90eabc5a2a322b90558497f015d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18032"/><div sID="gen36964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18032"/><hi type="bold">12. they all ... damned--</hi>rather as Greek, "that all," &c. He here states the general proposition which applies specially to Antichrist's adherents. Not all in the Church of Rome, or other anti-Christian systems, shall be damned, but only "all who believed not the truth," when offered to them, "but had pleasure in unrighteousness" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Ro 1:32</reference>; 2:8). Love of unrighteousness being the great obstacle to believing the truth. <div eID="gen36964" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7c8ff475fc8578ed6fb6b78fa9fa73fe56904f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18033"/><div sID="gen36965" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18033"/><hi type="bold">13. But--</hi>In delightful contrast to the damnation of the lost (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:12</reference>) stands the "salvation" of Paul's converts.<div eID="gen36965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are bound--</hi>in duty (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.3">2Th 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thanks ... to God--</hi>not to ourselves, your ministers, nor to you, our converts.<div eID="gen36967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beloved of the Lord--</hi>Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Ro 8:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.25">25</reference>). Elsewhere God the Father is said to love us (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.16">2Th 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.4">Ep 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col 3:12</reference>). Therefore Jesus and the Father are one.<div eID="gen36968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the beginning--</hi>"before the foundation of the world" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>); in contrast to those that shall "worship the beast, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world" (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>). Some of the oldest manuscripts read as English Version, but other oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read, "as first-fruits." The Thessalonians were among the first converts in Europe (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.5">Ro 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.15">1Co 16:15</reference>). In a more general sense, it occurs in <reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Re 14:4</reference>; so I understand it here including the more restricted sense.<div eID="gen36969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chosen you--</hi>The Greek, is not the ordinary word for "elected," implying His eternal selection; but taken for Himself, implying His having adopted them in His eternal purpose. It is found in the Septuagint (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.7">De 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.15">10:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>rather as Greek, "in sanctification" as the element in which the choice to salvation had place (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>), standing in contrast to the "unrighteousness," the element in which Antichrist's followers are given over by God to damnation (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen36971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the Spirit--</hi>wrought by the Spirit who sanctifies all the elect people of God, first by eternally consecrating them to perfect holiness in Christ, once for all, next by progressively imparting it.<div eID="gen36972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">belief of the truth--</hi>contrasted with "believed not the truth" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen36973" type="x-p"/>
entries.91fb6b60c766d3b9a788eaa49df9e873c282755d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18034"/><div sID="gen36974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18034"/><hi type="bold">14. you--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "us."<div eID="gen36974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by our gospel--</hi>"through" the Gospel which we preach.<div eID="gen36975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to ... glory--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference> it was "salvation," that is, deliverance from all evil, of body and soul (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.9">1Th 5:9</reference>); here it is positive good, even "glory," and that "the glory of our Lord Jesus" Himself, which believers are privileged to share with Him (<reference osisRef="John.17.22">Joh 17:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Ro 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">2Ti 2:10</reference>). <div eID="gen36976" type="x-p"/>
entries.0697e9fde8de150b27cd4408858d42e9b8c43bd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18035"/><div sID="gen36977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18035"/><hi type="bold">15. Therefore--</hi>God's sovereign choice of believers, so far from being a ground for inaction on their part, is the strongest incentive to action and perseverance in it. Compare the argument, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Php 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>, "Work out your own salvation, FOR it is God which worketh in you," &c. We cannot fully explain this in theory; but to the sincere and humble, the practical acting on the principle is plain. "Privilege first, duty afterwards" [Edmunds].<div eID="gen36977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand fast--</hi>so as not to be "shaken or troubled" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen36978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hold--</hi>so as not to let go. Adding nothing, subtracting nothing [Bengel]. The Thessalonians had not held fast his oral instructions but had suffered themselves to be imposed upon by pretended spirit-revelations, and words and letters pretending to be from Paul (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>), to the effect that "the day of the Lord was instantly imminent."<div eID="gen36979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">traditions--</hi>truths delivered and transmitted orally, or in writing (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6">2Th 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.2">1Co 11:2</reference>; Greek, "traditions"). The Greek verb from which the noun comes, is used by Paul in <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1Co 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">15:3</reference>. From the three passages in which "tradition" is used in a good sense, Rome has argued for her accumulation of uninspired traditions, virtually overriding God's Word, while put forward as of co-ordinate authority with it. She forgets the ten passages (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.2">Mt 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.6">3, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.7.3">Mr 7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.8">5, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.13">9, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.14">Ga 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>) stigmatizing man's uninspired traditions. Not even the apostles' sayings were all inspired (for example, Peter's dissimulation, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.11-Gal.2.14">Ga 2:11-14</reference>), but only when they claimed to be so, as in their words afterwards embodied in their canonical writings. Oral inspiration was necessary in their case, until the canon of the written Word should be complete; they proved their possession of inspiration by miracles wrought in support of the new revelation, which revelation, moreover, accorded with the existing Old Testament revelation; an additional test needed besides miracles (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.6">De 13:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.11">Ac 17:11</reference>). When the canon was complete, the infallibility of the living men was transferred to the written Word, now the sole unerring guide, interpreted by the Holy Spirit. Little else has come down to us by the most ancient and universal tradition save this, the all-sufficiency of Scripture for salvation. Therefore, by tradition, we are constrained to cast off all tradition not contained in, or not provable by, Scripture. The Fathers are valuable witnesses to historical facts, which give force to the intimations of Scripture: such as the Christian Lord's day, the baptism of infants, and the genuineness of the canon of Scripture. Tradition (in the sense of human testimony) cannot establish a doctrine, but can authenticate a fact, such as the facts just mentioned. Inspired tradition, in Paul's sense, is not a supplementary oral tradition completing our written Word, but it is identical with the written Word now complete; then the latter not being complete, the tradition was necessarily in part oral, in part written, and continued so until, the latter being complete before the death of St. John, the last apostle, the former was no longer needed. Scripture is, according to Paul, the complete and sufficient rule in all that appertains to making "the man of God perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2Ti 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">17</reference>). It is by leaving Paul's God-inspired tradition for human traditions that Rome has become the forerunner and parent of the Antichrist. It is striking that, from this very chapter denouncing Antichrist, she should draw an argument for her "traditions" by which she fosters anti-Christianity. Because the apostles' oral word was as trustworthy as their written word, it by no means follows that the oral word of those not apostles is as trustworthy as the written word of those who were apostles or inspired evangelists. No tradition of the apostles except their written word can be proved genuine on satisfactory evidence. We are no more bound to accept implicitly the Fathers' interpretations of Scripture, because we accept the Scripture canon on their testimony, than we are bound to accept the Jews' interpretation of the Old Testament, because we accept the Old Testament canon on their testimony.<div eID="gen36980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our epistle--</hi>as distinguished from a "letter AS from us," <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>, namely, that purports to be from us, but is not. He refers to his first Epistle to the Thessalonians. <div eID="gen36981" type="x-p"/>
entries.56a735ad988eb8595cc7d019c6dec348cff41bd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18036"/><div sID="gen36982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18036"/><hi type="bold">16-17. himself--</hi>by His own might, as contrasted with our feebleness; ensuring the efficacy of our prayer. Here our Lord Jesus stands first; in <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.11">1Th 3:11</reference>, "God our Father."<div eID="gen36982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which ... loved us--</hi>in the work of our redemption. Referring both to our Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Ro 8:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>) and God our Father (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen36983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting consolation--</hi>not transitory, as worldly consolations in trials (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.39">39</reference>). This for all time present, and then "good hope" for the future [Alford].<div eID="gen36984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through grace--</hi>rather as Greek "IN grace"; to be joined to "hath given." Grace is the element in which the gift was made. <div eID="gen36985" type="x-p"/>

entries.0d3f54e58a2c4843051d903c845beef2d2048a04: <div eID="gen51325" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51326" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51327" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51327" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51326" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51328" type="x-p"/> He exhorts the Thessalonians to stand fast in the faith, and not to be alarmed at the rumors they heard concerning the sudden coming of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Thes.2.1">2Thes 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Thes.2.2">2Thes 2:2</reference>. Because, previously to this coming, there would be a great apostasy from the true faith, and a manifestation of a son of perdition, of whose unparalleled presumption he gives an awful description; as well as of his pernicious success among men, and the means which he would use to deceive and pervert the world; and particularly those who do not receive the love of the truth, but have pleasure in unrighteousness, <reference osisRef="2Thes.2.3-2Thes.2.12">2Thes 2:3-12</reference>. He thanks God for their steadfastness; shows the great privileges to which they were called; and prays that they may be comforted and established in every good word and work, <reference osisRef="2Thes.2.13-2Thes.2.17">2Thes 2:13-17</reference>. <div eID="gen51328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51329" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51330" type="x-p"/> We beseech you - by the coming of our Lord - It is evident that the Thessalonians, incited by deceived or false teachers, had taken a wrong meaning out of the words of the first epistle, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.15">1Thes 4:15</reference>, etc., concerning the day of judgment; and were led then to conclude that that day was at hand; and this had produced great confusion in the Church: to correct this mistake, the apostle sent them this second letter, in which he shows that this day must be necessarily distant, because a great work is to be done previously to its appearing. <div eID="gen51330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51331" type="x-p"/> Of the day of general judgment he had spoken before, and said that it should come as a thief in the night, i.e. when not expected; but he did not attempt to fix the time, nor did he insinuate that it was either near at hand, or far off. Now, however, he shows that it must necessarily be far off, because of the great transactions which must take place before it can come.
entries.2657df02121c630b2ae124fa6d436e20aa783ee7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51332" type="x-p"/> Be not soon shaken in mind - Απο του νοος· From the mind; i.e. that they should retain the persuasion they had of the truths which he had before delivered to them; that they should still hold the same opinions, and hold fast the doctrines which they had been taught. <div eID="gen51332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51333" type="x-p"/> Neither by spirit - Any pretended revelation. <div eID="gen51333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51334" type="x-p"/> Nor by word - Any thing which any person may profess to have heard the apostle speak. <div eID="gen51334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51335" type="x-p"/> Nor by letter - Either the former one which he had sent, some passages of which have been misconceived and misconstrued; or by any other letter, as from us - pretending to have been written by us, the apostles, containing predictions of this kind. There is a diversity of opinion among critics concerning this last clause, some supposing that it refers simply to the first epistle; others supposing that a forged epistle is intended. I have joined the two senses. The word σαλευθηναι, to be shaken, signifies to be agitated as a ship at sea in a storm, and strongly marks the confusion and distress which the Thessalonians had felt in their false apprehension of this coming of Christ. <div eID="gen51335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51336" type="x-p"/> As that the day of Christ is at hand - In the preface to this epistle I have given a general view of the meaning of the phrase the coming of Christ. Now the question is: Whether does the apostle mean, the coming of Christ to execute judgment upon the Jews, and destroy their polity, or his coming at the end of time, to judge the world? There are certainly many expressions in the following verses that may be applied indifferently to either, and some seem to apply to the one, and not to the other; and yet the whole can scarcely be so interpreted as to suit any one of these comings exclusively. This is precisely the case with the predictions of our Lord relative to these great events; one is used to point out and illustrate the other. On this ground I am led to think that the apostle, in the following confessedly obscure words, has both these in view, speaking of none of them exclusively; for it is the custom of the inspired penmen, or rather of that Spirit by which they spoke, to point out as many certain events by one prediction as it was possible to do, and to choose the figures, metaphors, and similes accordingly; and thus, from the beginning, God has pointed out the things that were not by the things that then existed, making the one the types or significations of the other. As the apostle spoke by the same Spirit, he most probably followed the same plan; and thus the following prophecy is to be interpreted and understood.
entries.21746af2a85771d4191de19209ba2763bc0937c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51337" type="x-p"/> Except there come a falling away first - We have the original word αποστασια in our word apostasy; and by this term we understand a dereliction of the essential principles of religious truth - either a total abandonment of Christianity itself, or such a corruption of its doctrines as renders the whole system completely inefficient to salvation. But what this apostasy means is a question which has not yet, and perhaps never will be, answered to general satisfaction. At present I shall content myself with making a few literal remarks on this obscure prophecy, and afterwards give the opinions of learned men on its principal parts. <div eID="gen51337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51338" type="x-p"/> That man of sin - Ὁ ανθρωπος της ἁμαρτιας· The same as the Hebrew expresses by איש און ish aven, and איש בליעל ish beliyaal; the perverse, obstinate, and iniquitous man. It is worthy of remark that, among the rabbins, Samael, or the devil, is called איש בליעל ואיש און ish beliyaal veish aven, the man of Belial, and the man of iniquity; and that these titles are given to Adam after his fall. <div eID="gen51338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51339" type="x-p"/> The son of perdition - Ὁ υἱος της απωλειας· The son of destruction; the same epithet that is given to Judas Iscariot, <reference osisRef="Joh.17.12">Joh 17:12</reference> (note). The son of perdition, and the man of sin, or, as some excellent MSS. and versions, with several of the fathers, read, ανθρωπος της ανομιας, the lawless man, see <reference osisRef="2Thes.2.8">2Thes 2:8</reference>, must mean the same person or thing. It is also remarkable that the wicked Jews are styled by Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>, בנים משחיתים benim mashchithim, "children of perdition;" persons who destroy themselves and destroy others.
