This, therefore, was the delay, until the career of the gospel should be completed, because a gracious invitation to salvation was first in order. <note n="656"> <div sID="gen128672" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">D’autant que l’ordre que Dieu vouloit tenir, requeroit que le monde premierement fust d’vne liberalite gratuite conuié a salut</foreign>;” — “Inasmuch as the order that God designed to maintain, required that the world should first of all be invited to salvation by a gracious liberality.”<div eID="gen128672" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence he adds, <hi type="italic">in his time</hi>, because vengeance was ripe after grace had been rejected. <note n="657"> <div sID="gen128673" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La droite saison de la vengeance estoit apres la grace reiette</foreign>;” — “The right season of vengeance was after grace had been rejected.”<div eID="gen128673" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen128671" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128668" osisID="2Thess.2.6" type="section"/>
entries.382ecee507b7c7d31943a36e2c78ab7e463224f0: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Thess.2.7" sID="gen128674" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7</hi><hi type="italic">. The mystery of iniquity</hi>. This is opposed to <hi type="italic">revelation;</hi> for as Satan had not yet gathered so much strength, as that Antichrist could openly oppress the Church, he says that he is carrying on secretly and clandestinely <note n="658"> <div sID="gen128676" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et comme par dessous terre</foreign>;” — “And as it were under ground.”<div eID="gen128676" type="x-p"/> </note> what he would do openly in his own time. He was therefore at that time secretly laying the foundations on which he would afterwards rear the edifice, as actually took place. And this tends to confirm more fully what I have already stated, that it is not one individual that is represented under the term Antichrist, but one kingdom, which extends itself through many ages. In the same sense, John says that Antichrist will come, but that there were already many in his time. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.2.18">1 John 2:18</reference>.) For he admonishes those who were then living to be on their guard against that deadly pestilence, which was at that time shooting up in various forms. For sects were rising up which were the seeds, as it were, of that unhappy weed which has well-nigh choked and destroyed God’s entire tillage. <note n="659"> <div sID="gen128677" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le bon blé que Dieu auoit seme en son champ</foreign>;” — “The good wheat that God had sown in his field.”<div eID="gen128677" type="x-p"/> </note> But although Paul conveys the idea of a secret manner of working, yet he has made use of the term <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> rather than any other, alluding to the mystery of salvation, of which he speaks elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.26">Colossians 1:26</reference>,) for he carefully insists on the struggle of repugnancy between the Son of God and this <hi type="italic">son of perdition</hi><div eID="gen128675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128678" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Only now withholding</hi>. While he makes both statements in reference to one person — that he will hold supremacy for a time, and that he will shortly be taken out of the way, I have no doubt that he refers to Antichrist; and the participle <hi type="italic">withholding</hi> must be explained in the future tense. <note n="660"> <div sID="gen128679" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Faut resoudre ce participe <hi type="italic">Tenant</hi> en vn temps futur <hi type="italic">Tiendra</hi></foreign>;” — “We must explain this participle, withholding, in the future tense — <hi type="italic">He will withhold</hi>.”<div eID="gen128679" type="x-p"/> </note> For he has, in my opinion, added this for the consolation of believers — that the reign of Antichrist will be temporary, the limits of it having been assigned to it by God; for believers might object — “Of what avail is it that the gospel is preached, if Satan is now hatching a tyranny that he is to exercise for ever?” He accordingly exhorts to patience, because God afflicts his Church only for a time, that he may one day afford it deliverance; and, on the other hand, the perpetuity of Christ’s reign must be considered, in order that believers may repose in it.<div eID="gen128678" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128674" osisID="2Thess.2.7" type="section"/>
entries.1cd425260f54d5c308293c2816e5a4b688d3e0cb:
8 And then will be revealed — that is, when that impediment (τὸ κατέχον) shall be removed; for he does not point out the time of revelation as being when he, who now holds the supremacy, will be taken out of the way, but he has an eye to what he had said before. For he had said that there was some hindrance in the way of Antichrist’s entering upon an open possession of the kingdom. He afterwards added, that he was already hatching a secret work of impiety. In the third place, he has interspersed consolation, on the ground that this tyranny would come to an end.
“Que sa tyrannie deuoit prendre fin quelque fois;” — “That his tyranny must at some time have an end.”
He now again repeats, that he
“Ce fils de perdition;” — “This son of perdition.”
who was as yet hidden, would be revealed in his time; and the repetition is with this view — that believers, being furnished with spiritual armor, may, nevertheless, fight vigorously under Christ,
“Sous l’enseigne de Christ;” — “Under Christ’s banner.”
and not allow themselves to be overwhelmed, although the deluge of impiety should thus overspread.
“Si outrageusement;” — “So outrageously.”
Whom the Lord. He had foretold the destruction of Antichrist’s reign; he now points out the manner of his destruction — that he will be reduced to nothing by the word of the Lord. It is uncertain, however, whether he speaks of the last appearance of Christ, when he will be manifested from heaven as the Judge. The words, indeed, seem to have this meaning, but Paul does not mean that Christ would accomplish this
“Cela tout;” — “All this.”
in one moment. Hence we must understand it in this sense — that Antichrist would be wholly and in every respect destroyed,
“Descomfit;” — “Defeated.”
when that final day of the restoration of all things shall arrive. Paul, however, intimates that Christ will in the mean time, by the rays which he will emit previously to his advent, put to flight the darkness in which Antichrist will reign, just as the sun, before he is seen by us, chases away the darkness of the night by the pouring forth of his rays.
“Estendant la vertu de ses rayons tout a l’enuiron;” — “Diffusing the virtue of his rays all around.”
This victory of the word, therefore, will shew itself in this world, for the spirit of his mouth simply means the word, as it also does in Isaiah 11:4, to which passage Paul seems to allude. For the Prophet there takes in the same sense the scepter of his mouth, and the breath of his lips, and he also furnishes Christ with these very arms, that he may rout his enemies. This is a signal commendation of true and sound doctrine — that it is represented as sufficient for putting an end to all impiety, and as destined to be invariably victorious, in opposition to all the machinations of Satan; as also when, a little afterwards, the proclamation of it is spoken of as Christ’s coming to us.
When Paul adds, the brightness of his coming, he intimates that the light of Christ’s presence will be such as will swallow up the darkness of Antichrist. In the mean time, he indirectly intimates, that Antichrist will be permitted to reign for a time, when Christ has, in a manner, withdrawn, as usually happens, whenever on his presenting himself we turn our back upon him. And, undoubtedly, that is a sad departure
“Vn triste et pitoyable department;” — “A sad and lamentable departure.”
of Christ, when he has taken away his light from men, which has been improperly and unworthily received,
“Laquelle ils auoyent reiettee ou receué irreueremment, et autrement qu’il n’appartenoit;” — “Which they had rejected or received irreverently, and otherwise than was befitting.”
in accordance with what follows. In the mean time Paul teaches, that by his presence alone all the elect of God will be abundantly safe, in opposition to all the subtleties of Satan.
2 Thessalonians 2:9-12
9 Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,
9. Cuius adventus est secundum operationem (vel, efficaciam) Satanae, in omni potentia, et signis et prodigiis mendacibus,
10. And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved.
10. Et in omni deceptione iniustitiae, in iis qui pereunt: pro eo quod dilectionem veritatis non sunt amplexi, ut salvi fierent.
11. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie:
11. Propterea mittet illis Deus operationem (vel, efficaciam) imposturae, ut credant mendacio:
12. That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
12. Ut iudicentur omnes qui non crediderunt veritati, sed oblectati sunt iniustitia.
entries.2a8dd678eb7f35302be799766403ba6eeb4bd338: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Thess.2.9" sID="gen128705" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9</hi> <hi type="italic">Whose coming</hi> He confirms what he has said by an argument from contraries. For as Antichrist cannot stand otherwise than through the impostures of Satan, he must necessarily vanish as soon as Christ shines forth. In fine, as it is only in darkness that he reigns, the dawn of the day puts to flight and extinguishes the thick darkness of his reign. We are now in possession of Paul’s design, for he meant to say, that Christ would have no difficulty in destroying the tyranny of Antichrist, which was supported by no resources but those of Satan. In the mean time, however, he points out the marks by which that <hi type="italic">wicked one </hi>may be distinguished. For after having spoken of the <hi type="italic">working</hi> or <hi type="italic">efficacy</hi> of Satan, he marks it out particularly when he says, <hi type="italic">in signs and lying wonders, and in all deceivableness</hi>. And assuredly, in order that this may be opposed to the kingdom of Christ, it must consist partly in false doctrine and errors, and partly in pretended miracles. For the kingdom of Christ consists of the doctrine of truth, and the power of the Spirit. Satan, accordingly, with the view of opposing Christ in the person of his Vicar, puts on Christ’s mask, <note n="670"> <div sID="gen128707" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et s’en desguise</foreign>;” — “And disguises himself with it.”<div eID="gen128707" type="x-p"/> </note> while he, nevertheless, at the same time chooses armor, with which he may directly oppose Christ. Christ, by the doctrine of his gospel, enlightens our minds in eternal life; Antichrist, trained up under Satan’s tuition, by wicked doctrine, involves the wicked in ruin; <note n="671"> <div sID="gen128708" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En ruine et perdition eternelle</foreign>;” — “In eternal ruin and perdition.”<div eID="gen128708" type="x-p"/> </note> Christ puts forth the power of his Spirit for salvation, and seals his gospel by miracles; the adversary, <note n="672"> <div sID="gen128709" type="x-p"/> Our author evidently means Antichrist, alluding to the term applied to him by Paul in the 4th verse.—<hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen128709" type="x-p"/> </note> by the efficacy of Satan, alienates us from the Holy Spirit, and by his enchantments confirms miserable men <note n="673"> <div sID="gen128710" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les poures aveugles</foreign>;” — “The poor blind.”<div eID="gen128710" type="x-p"/> </note> in error.<div eID="gen128706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128711" type="x-p"/>He gives the name of <hi type="italic">miracles of falsehood</hi>, not merely to such as are falsely and deceptively contrived by cunning men with a view to impose upon the simple — a kind of deception with which all Papacy abounds, for they are a part of his power which he has previously touched upon; but takes falsehood as consisting in this, that Satan draws to a contrary end works which otherwise are truly works of God, and abuses miracles so as to obscure God’s glory. <note n="674"> <div sID="gen128712" type="x-p"/> It is observed by Dr. Manton, in his Sermons on 2d Thess. that “there are seven points in Popery that are sought to be confirmed by Miracles.—1. Pilgrimages. 2. Prayers for the Dead. 3. Purgatory. 4. The Invocation of Saints. 5. The Adoration of Images. 6. The Adoration of the Host. 7. The Primacy of the Pope.” —<hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen128712" type="x-p"/> </note> In the mean time, however, there can be no doubt, that he deceives by means of enchantments—an example of which we have in Pharaoh’s magicians. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.7.11">Exodus 7:11</reference>.)<div eID="gen128711" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128705" osisID="2Thess.2.9" type="section"/>
entries.693b8f8cdac0f1f043e6c36efba32a91f4e9d446: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Thess.2.10" sID="gen128713" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10</hi> <hi type="italic">In those that perish</hi>. He limits the power of Satan, as not being able to injure the elect of God, just as Christ, also, exempts them from this danger. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.24">Matthew 24:24</reference>.) From this it appears, that Antichrist has not so great power otherwise than by his permission. Now, this consolation was necessary. For all the pious, but for this, would of necessity be overpowered with fear, if they saw a yawning gulf pervading the whole path, along which they must pass. Hence Paul, however he may wish them to be in a state of anxiety, that they may be on their guard, lest by excessive carelessness they should fall back, nay, even throw themselves into ruin, does, nevertheless, bid them cherish good hope, inasmuch as Satan’s power is bridled, that he may not be able to involve any but the wicked in ruin.<div eID="gen128714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128715" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Because they received not the love</hi>. Lest the wicked should complain that they perish innocently, <note n="675"> <div sID="gen128716" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sans cause et estans innocens</foreign>;” — “Without cause, and being innocent.”<div eID="gen128716" type="x-p"/> </note> and that they have been appointed to death rather from cruelty on the part of God, than from any fault on their part, Paul shews on what good grounds it is that so severe vengeance from God is to come upon them — because they have not received in the temper of mind with which they ought the truth which was presented to them, nay more, of their own accord refused salvation. And from this appears more clearly what I have already stated — that the gospel required to be preached to the world before God would give Satan so much permission, for he would never have allowed his temple to be so basely profaned, <note n="676"> <div sID="gen128717" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vileinement et horriblement</foreign>;” — “Basely and horribly.”<div eID="gen128717" type="x-p"/> </note> had he not been provoked by extreme ingratitude on the part of men. In short, Paul declares that Antichrist will be the minister of God’s righteous vengeance against those who, being called to salvation, have rejected the gospel, and have preferred to apply their mind to impiety and errors. Hence there is no reason why Papists should now object, that it is at variance with the clemency of Christ to cast off his Church in this manner. For though the domination of Antichrist has been cruel, none have perished but those who were deserving of it, nay more, did of their own accord <hi type="italic">choose death</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Prov.8.36">Proverbs 8:36</reference>.) And unquestionably, while the voice of the Son of God has sounded forth everywhere, it finds the ears of men deaf, nay obstinate, <note n="677"> <div sID="gen128718" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Eudurcies et obstinees</foreign>;” — “Hardened and obstinate.”<div eID="gen128718" type="x-p"/> </note> and while a profession of Christianity is common, there are, nevertheless, few that have truly and heartily given themselves to Christ. Hence it is not to be wondered, if similar vengeance quickly follows such a criminal <note n="678"> <div sID="gen128719" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Si execrable</foreign>;” — “So execrable.”<div eID="gen128719" type="x-p"/> </note> contempt.<div eID="gen128715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128720" type="x-p"/>It is asked whether the punishment of blindness does not fall on any but those who have on set purpose rebelled against the gospel. I answer, that this special judgment by which God has avenged open contumacy, <note n="679"> <div sID="gen128721" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Le mespris orgueilleux de sa Parolle</foreign>;” — “Proud contempt of his Word.”<div eID="gen128721" type="x-p"/> </note> does not stand in the way of his striking down with stupidity, <note n="680"> <div sID="gen128722" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Estourdissement et stupidite</foreign>;” — “Giddiness and stupidity.”<div eID="gen128722" type="x-p"/> </note> as often as seems good to him, those that have never heard a single word respecting Christ, for Paul does not discourse in a general way as to the reasons why God has from the beginning permitted Satan to go at large with his falsehoods, but as to what a horrible vengeance impends over gross despisers of new and previously unwonted grace. <note n="681"> <div sID="gen128723" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est ascauoir de l’Euangile</foreign>;” — “That is, of the Gospel.”<div eID="gen128723" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen128720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128724" type="x-p"/>He uses the expression — <hi type="italic">receiving the love of the truth</hi>, to mean — applying the mind to the love of it. Hence we learn that faith is always conjoined with a sweet and voluntary reverence for God, because we do not properly believe the word of God, unless it is lovely and pleasant to us.<div eID="gen128724" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128713" osisID="2Thess.2.10" type="section"/>
entries.fbaee497ae16f0e7bb5c445016fd5dbe7178e961: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Thess.2.11" sID="gen128725" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11</hi> <hi type="italic"> The working of delusion</hi>. He means that errors will not merely have a place, but the wicked will be blinded, so that they will rush forward to ruin without consideration. For as God enlightens us inwardly by his Spirit, that his doctrine may be efficacious in us, and opens our eyes and hearts, that it may make its way thither, so by a righteous judgment he delivers over to a <hi type="italic">reprobate mind </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.28">Romans 1:28</reference>) those whom he has appointed to destruction, that with closed eyes and a senseless mind, they may, as if bewitched, deliver themselves over to Satan and his ministers to be deceived. And assuredly we have a notable specimen of this in the Papacy. No words can express how monstrous a sink of errors <note n="682"> <div sID="gen128727" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quel monstrueux et horrible retrait d’erreurs</foreign>;” — “What a monstrous and horrible nest of errors.”<div eID="gen128727" type="x-p"/> </note> there is <hi type="italic">there</hi>, how gross and shameful an absurdity of superstitions there is, and what delusions at variance with common sense. None that have even a moderate taste of sound doctrine, can think of such monstrous things without the greatest horror. How, then, could the whole world be lost in astonishment at them, were it not that men have been struck with blindness by the Lord, and converted, as it were, into stumps?<div eID="gen128726" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128725" osisID="2Thess.2.11" type="section"/>
entries.4a13bcb93c3d6fd5ae7b87862d20fa9c2939caa3:
12 That all may be condemned. That is, that they may receive the punishment due to their impiety. Thus, those that perish have no just ground to expostulate with God, inasmuch as they have obtained what they sought. For we must keep in view what is stated in Deuteronomy 13:3, that the hearts of men are subjected to trial, when false doctrines come abroad, inasmuch as they have no power except among those who do not love God with a sincere heart. Let those, then, who take pleasure in unrighteousness, reap the fruit of it. When he says all, he means that contempt of God finds no excuse in the great crowd and multitude of those who refuse to obey the gospel, for God is the Judge of the whole world, so that he will inflict punishment upon a hundred thousand, no less than upon one individual.
The participle εὐδοκήσαντες (taking pleasure) means (so to speak) a voluntary inclination to evil, for in this way every excuse is cut off from the ungrateful, when they take so much pleasure in unrighteousness, as to prefer it to the righteousness of God. For by what violence will they say that they have been impelled to alienate themselves by a mad revolt
“En se reuoltant malicieusement;” — “By revolting maliciously.”
from God, towards whom they were led by the guidance of nature? It is at least manifest that they willingly and knowingly lent an ear to falsehoods.
2 Thessalonians 2:13-14
13. But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:
13. Nos autem debemus gratias agere Deo semper de vobis, fratres dilecti a Domino, quia elegit vos Deus ab initio in salutem, in sanctificatione Spiritus, et fide veritatis:
14. Whereunto he called you by our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
14. Quo vocavit vos per evangelium nostrum, in possessionem gloriae (vel, gloriosam) Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
entries.cc5fa9c619b1342a26e76b63d802a4b243aa9ce1: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Thess.2.13" sID="gen128739" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13</hi> <hi type="italic">But we are bound to give thanks</hi>. He now separates more openly the Thessalonians from the reprobate, that their faith may not waver from fear of the revolt that was to take place. At the same time, he had it in view to consult, not <hi type="italic">their</hi> welfare only, but also that of posterity. <note n="684"> <div sID="gen128741" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais aussi pour les autres fideles, qui viendroyent apres</foreign>;” — “But also for other believers, who should come after.”<div eID="gen128741" type="x-p"/> </note> And he does not merely confirm them that they may not fall over the same precipice with the world, but by this comparison he extols the more the grace of God towards them, in that, while they see almost the whole world hurried forward to death at the same time, as if by a violent tempest, they are, by the hand of God, maintained in a quiet and secure condition of life. <note n="685"> <div sID="gen128742" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En vn estat ferme et paisible, qui mene a la vie</foreign>;” — “In a secure and peaceable condition, which leads to life.”<div eID="gen128742" type="x-p"/> </note> Thus we must contemplate the Judgments of God upon the reprobate in such a way that they may be, as it were, mirrors to us for considering his mercy towards us. For we must draw this conclusion, that it is owing solely to the singular grace of God that we do not miserably perish with them.<div eID="gen128740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128743" type="x-p"/>He calls them <hi type="italic">beloved of the Lord</hi>, for this reason, that they may the better consider that the sole reason why they are exempted from the almost universal overthrow of the world, was because God exercised towards them unmerited love. Thus Moses admonished the Jews —<div eID="gen128743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128744" type="x-p"/>“God did not elevate you so magnificently because ye were more powerful than others, or were numerous, but because he loved your fathers.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deuteronomy 7:7-8</reference>.)<div eID="gen128744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128745" type="x-p"/>For, when we hear the term <hi type="italic">love</hi>, that statement of John must immediately occur to our mind — <hi type="italic">Not that we first loved him</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.4.19">1 John 4:19</reference>.) In short, Paul here does two things; for he confirms faith, lest the pious should give way from being overcome with fear, and he exhorts them to gratitude, that they may value so much the higher the mercy of God towards them.<div eID="gen128745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128746" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Hath chosen you</hi>. He states the reason why all are not involved and swallowed up in the same ruin — because Satan has no power over any that God has chosen, so as to prevent them from being saved, though heaven and earth were to be confounded. This passage is read in various ways.<div eID="gen128746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128747" type="x-p"/>The old interpreter has rendered it <hi type="italic">first-fruits</hi>, <note n="686"> <div sID="gen128748" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Primitias</hi></foreign>. Wiclif (1380) following, as he is wont, the reading of the Vulgate, renders it “the first fruytis.”<div eID="gen128748" type="x-p"/> </note> as being in the Greek <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀπαρχήν</foreign>; but as almost all the Greek manuscripts have <foreign xml:lang="el">απ᾿ ἀρχὢς</foreign>, I have in preference followed this reading. Should any one prefer <hi type="italic">first-fruits</hi>, the meaning will be, that believers have been, as it were, set aside for a sacred offering, by a metaphor taken from the ancient custom of the law. Let us, however, hold by what is more generally received, that he says that the Thessalonians were <hi type="italic">chosen from the beginning</hi><div eID="gen128747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128749" type="x-p"/>Some understand the meaning to be, that they had been called among the first; but this is foreign to Paul’s meaning, and does not accord with the connection of the passage. For he does not merely exempt from fear a few individuals, who had been led to Christ immediately on the commencement of the gospel, but this consolation belongs to all the elect of God, without exception. When, therefore, he says <hi type="italic">from the beginning</hi>, he means that there is no danger lest their salvation, which is founded on God’s eternal election, should be overthrown, whatever tumultuous changes may occur. “However Satan may mix and confound all things in the world, your salvation, notwithstanding, has been placed on a footing of safety, prior to the creation of the world.” Here, therefore, is the true port of safety, that God, who elected us of old, <note n="687"> <div sID="gen128750" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Des le commencement</foreign>;” — “From the beginning.”<div eID="gen128750" type="x-p"/> </note> will deliver us from all the evils that threaten us. For we are elected to salvation; we shall, therefore, be safe from destruction. But as it is not for us to penetrate into God’s secret counsel, to seek <hi type="italic">there</hi> assurance of our salvation, he specifies signs or tokens of election, which should suffice us for the assurance of it.<div eID="gen128749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128751" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In sanctification of the spirit</hi>, says he, <hi type="italic">and belief of the truth</hi>. This may be explained in two ways, <hi type="italic">with sanctification</hi>, or <hi type="italic">by sanctification</hi>. It is not of much importance which of the two you select, as it is certain <note n="688"> <div sID="gen128752" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">S. Paul ne vent autre chose, sinon apres auoir parlé de l’election de Dieu, adiouster maintenant des signes plus prochains qui nous la manifestent</foreign>;” — “St. Paul means simply, after having spoken of the election of God, to add now those nearer tokens which manifest it to us.”<div eID="gen128752" type="x-p"/> </note> that Paul meant simply to introduce, in connection with election, those nearer tokens which manifest to us what is in its own nature incomprehensible, and are conjoined with it by an indissoluble tie. Hence, in order that we may know that we are elected by God, there is no occasion to inquire as to what he decreed before the creation of the world, but we find in ourselves a satisfactory proof if he has sanctified us by his Spirit, — if he has enlightened us in the faith of his gospel. For the gospel is an evidence to us of our adoption, and the Spirit seals it, and those that are <hi type="italic">led by the Spirit are the sons of God</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.14">Romans 8:14</reference>,) and he who by faith possesses Christ has everlasting life. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.5.12">1 John 5:12</reference>.) These things must be carefully observed, lest, overlooking the revelation of God’s will, with which he bids us rest satisfied, we should plunge into a profound labyrinth from a desire to take it from his secret counsel, from the investigation of which he draws us aside. Hence it becomes us to rest satisfied with the faith of the gospel, and that grace of the Spirit by which we have been regenerated. And by this means is refuted the wickedness <note n="689"> <div sID="gen128753" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">La meschancete horrible</foreign>;” — “The horrible wickedness.”<div eID="gen128753" type="x-p"/> </note> of those who make the election of God a pretext for every kind of iniquity, while Paul connects it with faith and regeneration in such a manner, that he would not have it judged of by us on any other grounds.<div eID="gen128751" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128739" osisID="2Thess.2.13" type="section"/>
entries.db96bf4099b0e4ae90795e6996b186245e377503:
14 To which he called us. He repeats the same thing, though in somewhat different terms. For the sons of God are not called otherwise than to the belief of the truth. Paul, however, meant to shew here how competent a witness he is for confirming that thing of which he was a minister. He accordingly puts himself forward as a surety, that the Thessalonians may not doubt that the gospel, in which they had been instructed by him, is the safety-bringing voice of God, by which they are aroused from death, and are delivered from the tyranny of Satan. He calls it his gospel, not as though it had originated with him,
“Non pas qu’il soit creu en son cerueau;” — “Not as though it had been contrived in his brain.”
but inasmuch as the preaching of it had been committed to him.
What he adds, to the acquisition or possession of the glory of Christ, may be taken either in an active or in a passive signification — either as meaning, that they are called in order that they may one day possess a glory in common with Christ, or that Christ acquired them with a view to his glory. And thus it will be a second means of confirmation that he will defend them, as being nothing less than his own inheritance, and, in maintaining their salvation, will stand forward in defense of his own glory; which latter meaning, in my opinion, suits better.
2 Thessalonians 2:15-17
15. Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
15. Itaque fratres, state, et tenete institutiones, quas didicistis vel per sermonem, vel per epistolam nostram.
16. Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, which hath loved us, and hath given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace,
16. Ipse vero Dominus noster Iesus Christus, et Deus, ac Pater noster, qui dilexcit nos, et dedit consolationem aeternam, et spem bonam per gratiam,
17. Comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work.
17. Consoletur corda vestra, et stabiliat vos in omni opere et sermone bono.
entries.21675830c46f9740d716a04bad13f93df413dad2: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Thess.2.15" sID="gen128767" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128768" type="x-p"/>He deduces this exhortation on good grounds from what goes before, inasmuch as our steadfastness and power of perseverance rest on nothing else than assurance of divine grace. When, however, God calls us to salvation, stretching forth, as it were, his hand to us; when Christ, by the doctrine of the gospel, presents himself to us to be enjoyed; when the Spirit is given us as a seal and earnest of eternal life, though the heaven should fall, we must, nevertheless, not become disheartened. Paul, accordingly, would have the Thessalonians stand, not merely when others continue to stand, but with a more settled stability; so that, on seeing almost all turning aside from the faith, and all things full of confusion, they will, nevertheless, retain their footing. And assuredly the calling of God ought to fortify us against all occasions of offense in such a manner, that not even the entire ruin of the world shall shake, much less overthrow, our stability.<div eID="gen128768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15</hi> <hi type="italic">Hold fast the institutions</hi>. Some restrict this to precepts of external polity; but this does not please me, for he points out the manner of standing firm. Now, to be furnished with invincible strength is a much higher thing than external discipline. Hence, in my opinion, he includes all doctrine under this term, as though he had said that they have ground on which they may stand firm, provided they persevere in sound doctrine, according as they had been instructed by him. I do not deny that the term <foreign xml:lang="el">παραδόσεις </foreign>is fitly applied to the ordinances which are appointed by the Churches, with a view to the promoting of peace and the maintaining of order, and I admit that it is taken in this sense when human traditions are treated of, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.6">Matthew 15:6</reference>.) Paul, however, will be found in the next chapter making use of the term <hi type="italic">tradition</hi>, as meaning the rule that he had laid down, and the very signification of the term is general. The context, however, as I have said, requires that it be taken here to mean the whole of that doctrine in which they had been instructed. For the matter treated of is the most important of all — that their faith may remain secure in the midst of a dreadful agitation of the Church.<div eID="gen128769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128770" type="x-p"/>Papists, however, act a foolish part in gathering from this that their traditions ought to be observed. They reason, indeed, in this manner — that if it was allowable for Paul to enjoin traditions, it was allowable also for other teachers; and that, if it was a pious thing <note n="691"> <div sID="gen128771" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Une bonne chose et saincte</foreign>;” — “A good thing and holy.”<div eID="gen128771" type="x-p"/> </note> to observe the former, the latter also ought not less to be observed. Granting them, however, that Paul speaks of precepts belonging to the external government of the Church, I say that they were, nevertheless, not contrived by him, but divinely communicated. For he declares elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.7.35">1 Corinthians 7:35</reference>,) that it was not his intention to ensnare consciences, as it was not lawful, either for himself, or for all the Apostles together. They act a still more ridiculous part in making it their aim to pass off, under this, the abominable sink of their own superstitions, as though they were the traditions of Paul. But farewell to these trifles, when we are in possession of Paul’s true meaning. And we may judge in part from this Epistle what traditions he here recommends, for he says — whether <hi type="italic">by word</hi>, that is, discourse, or <hi type="italic">by epistle</hi>. Now, what do these Epistles contain but pure doctrine, which overturns to the very foundation the whole of the Papacy, and every invention that is at variance with the simplicity of the Gospel?<div eID="gen128770" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Thess.2.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128767" osisID="2Thess.2.15" type="section"/>
entries.9dc9104e1730702801c5a5c1ee85b73227e78fc3:
16 Now the Lord himself. When he ascribes to Christ a work altogether Divine, and represents him, in common with the Father, as the Author of the choicest blessings, as we have in this a clear proof of the divinity of Christ, so we are admonished, that we cannot obtain anything from God unless we seek it in Christ himself: and when he asks that God may give him those things which he had enjoined, he shews clearly enough how little influence exhortations have, unless God inwardly move and affect our hearts. Unquestionably there will be but an empty sound striking upon the ear, if doctrine does not receive efficacy from the Spirit.
What he afterwards adds, who hath loved you, and hath given consolation, etc., relates to confidence in asking; for he would have the Thessalonians feel persuaded that God will do what he prays for. And from what does he prove this? Because he once shewed that they were dear to him, while he has already conferred upon them distinguished favors, and in this manner has bound himself to them for the time to come. This is what he means by everlasting consolation. The term hope, also, has the same object in view — that they may confidently expect a never-failing continuance of gifts. But what does he ask? That God may sustain their hearts by his consolation; for this is his office, to keep them from giving way through anxiety or distrust; and farther, that he may give them perseverance, both in a pious and holy course of life, and in sound doctrine; for I am of opinion, that it is rather of this than of common discourse that he speaks, so that this agrees with what goes before.
CHAPTER 3
2 Thessalonians 3:1-5
1. Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you:
1. Quod reliquum est, orate fratres pro nobis: ut sermo Domini currat et glorificetur, quemadmodum et apud vos;
2. And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.
2. Et ut liberemur ab importunis et malignis hominibus: non enim omnium est fides.
3. But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil.
3. Fidelis autem Dominus, qui confirmabit vos, et custodiet a maligno.
4. And we have confidence in the Lord touching you, that ye both do and will do the things which we command you.
4. Confidimus autem in Domino de vobis, quod quae vobis praecipimus, et facitis, et facturi estis.
5. And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patient waiting for Christ.
5. Dominus autem dirigat corda vestra in dilectionem Dei, et exspectationem Christi.

entries.4dda0bb7bb0f8a77abe31967f10d68594e69b3a3:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="2" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. II.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 NOW we beseech you brethren <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That he might the better perswade, he calls them brethren, and besee<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches them, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">And next, conjures them, using the form of an Oath, <ns0:hi>by the coming of our Lord Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi> &c. We conjure men either by what they love, or by what they fear; as they would enjoy the one, or avoid the other. The coming of Christ was what they desired and rejoyced in, as that which would bring rest to them and tribulation to their Adversaries: And by this he doth therefore beseech, or adjure them; and therefore we must understand this of Christ last coming, as the word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, in the Text is still applyed to this coming, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.19. and 3.13. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and not of his coming to destroy the Jewish Church and State, for that coming was at hand.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> our gathering together unto him <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>into him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">At his last coming, when the whole Body of Christ shall be ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thered to him, to meet him in the Air, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.17. and then the sence is, As ye hope ever to see such a blessed meeting, and to be of that number, so take heed of this opinion. Yet some read the Text otherwise, because in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> it is not <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, but <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and so the same with <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, not we beseech you <ns0:hi>by,</ns0:hi> but concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together unto him, as denoting only the Sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ject matter treated of: I prefer the former, and so the Apostle conjures them not to be soon shaken in mind, but to stand fast in the truth about the Doctrine of Christs coming, which they had been taught, and very lately taught, and therefore it was the greater evil to be <ns0:hi>soon shaken</ns0:hi>; as the Apostle upbraids the <ns0:hi>Galatians, Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.6. and God the <ns0:hi>Israelites, Psal.</ns0:hi> 106.13.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Apostle now comes to refute the opinion that some at least of these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> had received, as if the day of Christ was near at hand. He having said, 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4.17. <ns0:hi>We which are alive, and remain, shall be caught up to meet the Lord in the air,</ns0:hi> &c. Then some might think his coming would be in the Apostles time, or some other way, they might fall into this conceit, and some do conceive this was the chief reason of the Apostles writing this Epistle. And because this mistake might be of dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gerous consequence, therefore he is very vehement and particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lar in refuting i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>: For hereupon they might be brought to question the truth of the whole Gospel when this should not come to pass: They might be unprepared for the sufferings that were to come upon the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hurch; their patience might fail in expecting this day, and their minds be doubting about the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of Christ at all. This opinion also would much narrow their thoughts about Christs Kingdom, and the enlarging of the Gospel among other Gentiles, And the prophane might abuse it to sensuality, as 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15 32. <ns0:hi>let us eat and drink.</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 24.4 Eph. 5.6. 1 Joh. 4.1.</ns0:note> That ye be not <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>easily.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> soon shaken in mind <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, It is an allusion to the Waves of the Sea that are tossed with the Winds, as false Doctrines tend to unsettle the mind, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.14. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 13.9. and to be establisht in the truth, is often commanded 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.13. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.1: <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.24, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And by mind here is either meant the faculty it self, and then the Apostle beseecheth them to keep company with their understanding, not to be removed from their mind. As false Doctrine is said to bewitch men, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.1. and to make men foolish, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 3. as madness is called <ns0:hi>amentia,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>dementia,</ns0:hi> as that which doth as it were dismind men, and corrupt the mind, and pervert the judgment, 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.8, 9. as <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iambres</ns0:hi> deceived the people by their Enchantments, as the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle there mentions: Or else, the Sentence and Judgment of the mind. And then they are beseeched to hold fast the right Judgment they had entertained about Christ's coming, and not to haesitate and waver about it, so the word is taken 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.16.</ns0:note>, or be troubled <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Alluding to Souldiers affrighted with a sudden alarm. We find the word <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 24.6. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 13.7. used in this allusion. And the opinion of Christs com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to be at hand might occasion this trouble in them, either lest they might be surprized by it, and unprepared for it, or by judging themselves mistaken in their former apprehensions about it; and those false Teachers that broach this Opinion, did also perhaps so represent this coming in such terrour as to cause this Trouble. As false Teachers in general are such as are said to cause trouble, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.7. and 5.12. Though the coming of Christ is in it self rather the Saints Hope and Joy, than ground of Trouble, as 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.10. and 4.18, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And it may be some did pretend for this Opinion the Spirit, or some Letter from the Apostle, either the former Epistle to them, or some Letter that was forged, or some word he had spoken or preached. And those words <ns0:hi>as from us</ns0:hi> may refer to all these: The Spirit <ns0:hi>as from us</ns0:hi>; or Word, <ns0:hi>as from us</ns0:hi>; or Letter, <ns0:hi>as from us.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, neither by spirit <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Some extraordinary Revelation of the Spirit, which the false Tea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chers pretended to, especially in the Primitive times, when they were more ordinary; as in the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.6. and the Churches of <ns0:hi>Galatia, Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.2, 5. some would pretend the Spirit that called Jesus accursed, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.3. and therefore the Apostle bids, <ns0:hi>Try the Spirit,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.1. <ns0:hi>Simon Magus</ns0:hi> pretended to it, and had his <ns0:hi>Helene, Montanus</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Paraclete, Mahomet</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Dove</ns0:hi>: And the man of sin pretends to this Spirit, though it is in truth the Spirit of Antichrist, 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4.3. and the Spirit of Satan in the next Chapter of this Epi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle, as was foretold that in the last times, there would arise seducing Spirits, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.1. As there was in the times of the Old Testament false Prophets that pretended to the Spirit; as 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 22.24. <ns0:hi>Micah</ns0:hi> 2.11. And the very Heathen would pretend to Divine Oracles, Inspirations, and Revelations, espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially their Kings and Lawgivers, as <ns0:hi>N<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ma Pompilius, Lycurgus,</ns0:hi> &c. and still there are Enthusiasts who make these pretences.</ns0:note>: nor by word <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, whereby some understand Calculation by Astro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />logical Rules, that the day of Christ was at hand; others render the word <ns0:hi>Reasoning</ns0:hi>; and so from the declining of the vigour of the Earth, and the nearer approach of the Sun to it, as <ns0:hi>Pto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lomy</ns0:hi> observed in his time, or some other Natural causes; they reasoned the coming of Christ, and the dissolution of the World to be nigh at hand; but rather we understand by it some word from the Apostles own mouth, which was pretended he had spoken, or preached some where, though not written. As the Church of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> pretends to Traditions, besides the written word, upon which they ground many of their Superstitions, and Idolatries, not warranted by Scripture. As the Jews had a second <ns0:hi>Mish<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eh,</ns0:hi> and their <ns0:hi>Cabbala,</ns0:hi> collected in part from the sayings of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> or some other of their Prophets, which they did not write.</ns0:note>, nor by letter <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Some Letter that was sent to them from some hand or other, or else by some forged Letter as from the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle himself, or his former Epistle misunderstood.</ns0:note>, as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> But is it not said that the day of the Lord, <ns0:hi>or the coming of the Lord is at hand,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.11. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 4.5. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 5.7, 8. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.7. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> The word used in those places, differs from this in the Text; for it signifies either that which is actually present, or very near it, as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.38. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.4. as that which is to be done presently, is spoken of as done, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17.4. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.7. or those places mean this coming is at hand, as to Gods account of time, though not as mans. And in that sence Christ saith, <ns0:hi>Behold I come quickly, Rev.</ns0:hi> 22.7. But the errour the Apostle warns them of, is, as if the coming of Christ would be in the Age, wherein they lived. The Apostles all said that the coming of the Lord was at hand, but their right meaning was perverted to a false sence, as seducers usually do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:524" />3 Let no man deceive you <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Here the Apostle urgeth again his charge against this errour, though in other words, and begins his arguments to refute it. He had adjur'd them not to be shaken, and here he cautions them against being deceived<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> (for the one makes way for the other;) so also <ns0:hi>not to be troubled, ver.</ns0:hi> 2. for troubled minds are apt to be made a prey, to seducers. And the caution in the Text proves that their shaking and trouble did arise from some deceivers that were amongst them, rather than any misunder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing of their own of what he wrote in the former Epi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle about Christs coming. To be shaken in mind is bad, but to be deceived, is worse; for it is a going out of the path, as the word signifies; and therefore his caution against it is uni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versal, both as to persons and waies: Let no man deceive you, though he pretend to Revelations, or is of the greatest Reputa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion in the Church.</ns0:note> by any means <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either of Craft, Flattery, pretending Love, or plausible Arguments, or mis-representing our words, or forging of Letters, or misinterpreting our Epistle to you, or any other part of Scripture, or feigned Miracles, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Then he enters the Arguments to confute it, which are 1. The Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral Apostasie. 2. The Revelation of the man of sin, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther of these are yet, nor will be in this Age; and yet <ns0:hi>that day shall not come,</ns0:hi> till these both first come.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:hi>that day shall not come,</ns0:hi> except there come a fal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling away first <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">There is a supple<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment in our Translation, for in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> it is only <ns0:hi>For, except there come a falling away first,</ns0:hi> &c. or an Apostacy, a recession, a departing, or a standing oft, as the word imports, so that Apostasie may be either good when it is from evil to good, or evil, when it is from good to evil. It is alwaies used in this latter sence in Scripture. Again it is either Civil or Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual: Civil, as when people fall off from the Civil Govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment they were under, and so some would sence the Text of the defection from the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Empire, the East part from the West, and the Ten Kingdoms that arose out of it, which was the Opinion of <ns0:hi>Hieron, Epist. ad Algasiam</ns0:hi>; but the Apostle writing to the Church speaks not of Civil Government, and the Affairs of State; and speaks of such an Apostacy which would give rise to the man of sin, and the Revelation of him. And this man of sin riseth up in the Church, not in the Civil State; and the consequence of this Apostacy is giving men up to strong de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lusions to believe a lye, and then follows their Damnation; and the cause of it is said to be, not receiving the Truth in the Love of it; so that it is not a Civil, but Spiritual Apostacy, as the word in Scripture is alwaies (I suppose so taken.) And it is not of a particular person, or of a particular Church, but a general Apostacy of the Church, though not of every indi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vidual. That Church that is afterwards called the Temple of God, where the man of sin sitteth, and is exalted above all that is called God, which cannot be in any particular Church, and would not the Apostle have specified that particular Church? neither is it some lesser Apostacy, which may befal the best Church; but such as would be eminent, call'd <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, that Apostasie greater than that of some believing Jews to Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />daism, or of some Christians to Nicholaitanisme, which some think is meant, much less can it be <ns0:hi>Caius Caesar,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Grotius</ns0:hi> in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terprets, or any one person, for the Apostle saith not Apostate, but Apostacy, else a man of sin could not rise out of it, and ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />alt himself above all that is called God, and Worshipped. It is an Apostacy from sound Doctrine, instituted Worship, Church-Government, and true Holiness of Life, as may be further con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidered afterwards; neither is the Apostacy all at once, but gra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dual; for out of it ariseth a man of sin, who grows up to this manhood by degrees, and sin and wickedness are not com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pleated at first as well as Holiness; much less is this Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stacy a falling off from the Church of <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> as some Papists affirm, and make the Reformation to be the Apostacy, which was a return from it, doth the man of sin rise out of the Ref<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>r<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mation? Did any of the first Reformers oppose and exalt themselves above all that is called God, or is Worshipped? Or, as God sat in the Temple of God, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> was any of their coming with all power, and signs, and lying-wonders? Or, did any of them forbid to Marry, and to abstain from Meats, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which is the character our Apostle gives of this Apostasie, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.1, 2, 3. neither is the <ns0:hi>Mahometan</ns0:hi> Religion this Apostasie, for <ns0:hi>Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />homet</ns0:hi> sitteth not in the Temple of God, neither is it the falling of the Converted Jews from the Jewish Church, to the Gospel Church; the Apostle would never call that an Apostacy.</ns0:note>, and that man of sin be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vealed <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The next Argument is from the revelation of the man of sin: This is also to precede Christs last coming, it is an <ns0:hi>Hebraism.</ns0:hi> A Warlike man is stiled a man of War, a bloody man, a man of bloods, a deceitful man, a man of deceit, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> so a man eminent in sin is here called a man of sin; not only personally so, but who doth promote sin, propagate it, countenance it, command it, Vid. <ns0:hi>Platina, Sigebert, Blonetas, Beuno Uspregensis, Matt. Paris.</ns0:hi> In sins of Omission, forbidding what God requireth, in sins of Commission, requiring, or allowing what God hath for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bidden. In sins of the first Table, corrupting Gods Worship by Superstition and Idolatry, taking Gods Name in vain by heartless Devotion, dissembling Piety, dispensing with Perjury and false Oaths, taking away the second Commandment, and the morality of the Fourth Commandment, and mak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing mens Faith and Obedience to rest upon an humane Authority, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> In sins of the second Table, to dispense with Duties belonging to Superiours and Inferiours; with Murder, Adultery, Fornication, Incest, Robbery, Lying, Equivocati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And besides all these; promoting a false Religion, and destroying the true by Fines, Imprisonments, Banishments, Tortures, Poysons, Massacre, Fire, and Fagot. And this man of sin is not a single person, but a company, order, and succession of men, because all are acted by the same Spirit, therefore called a man, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 10.18. The <ns0:hi>man of the Earth</ns0:hi> is all, men of an Earthly Spirit, and a man of the Field is men whose minds and employments are in the Field, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 25.27. or it is a sinful state. As the Civil State of the four Monarchies in <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> is represented by four single Beasts, and the Antichristi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />an State by a Beast rising out of the Sea, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.1. so by man of sin is meant a sinful State, which though it consisteth of many People and Nations, yet being under the influence and Government of one man may be also stiled the Man of Sin upon that account; <ns0:hi>Impietatis Coryphaeus. Moulin.</ns0:hi> And because the sin of the whole Community is chiefly centred in him, and springs out from him; A man in whom is the Fountain of all sins, <ns0:hi>Hierom ad Algasiam</ns0:hi>: And the sin of this State is called a Myste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry of Iniquity, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7. and so differing from the sin in all other political States; and therefore may well be judged to be the same with the Whore sitting on many Waters, that hath Myste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry written in her Forehead, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.1, 5. and as no Exposi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor takes the <ns0:hi>Whore</ns0:hi> to be meant of a single Woman, and the true Apostolick Church is represented by a Woman in Travel, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 12.1. Why then should we take the Man of Sin to be a single Man, as the Papists do<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> a Jew of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Dan,</ns0:hi> that shall erect his Kingdom and Temple in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> seduce the Jews, continue three years and an half, make great havock of the Church to be opposed by <ns0:hi>Enoch</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Elias</ns0:hi>: and is to come a little before the end of the World. Ridiculous! neither can this man of sin be <ns0:hi>Simon Magus</ns0:hi> and his followers<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for he was revealed in the Apostles time, seeing the Mystery of Iniquity belonging to this man of sin began to work in the Apostles dayes, as <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7. and he is the same whom St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> calls Anti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />christ, 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2.18. and the Spirit of Antichrist began to be in the World in his time, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4.3. and the Nations are to be made drunk with the Cup of his Fornication, and to serve and obey him, <ns0:hi>&c. Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.8. and 17.4. All which requires more time than is allotted by them: But they set him a great way off, that none may suspect him to be among themselves; but he that will compare the Church of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> in the Apostle <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s times with what it is now, and the Doctrine of the Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cil of <ns0:hi>Trent</ns0:hi> with that laid down in his Epistle to the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> may say, How is the Faithful City become an Harlot? And this man of sin <ns0:hi>is to be revealed also,</ns0:hi> which shews that he is not a single person, not yet born: Revealing relates not so much to a person, as a thing; in particular to the mystery of Iniquity, mentioned <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7. his revealing is either <ns0:hi>quoad existentiam,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>apparentiam.</ns0:hi> The former is meant here, and the latter, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 8. He grows up into an existence, as the Apostacy grows, as Ver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />min grows out of putrefaction. As the Churches Purity, Faith, Love, Holiness declined, and as Pride, Ambition, Covetousness, Luxury prevailed, so he grew up: And which was the direct point and time of his full revelation in this first sence is conjectur'd by many, but determin'd by none; it is most generally refer'd to the time of <ns0:hi>Boniface</ns0:hi> the 3<ns0:hi>d.</ns0:hi> to whom <ns0:hi>Phocas</ns0:hi> granted the stile of Oecumenical Bishop and to the Church of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> to be the Mother Church. But as the Apostasie brings forth this man of sin, so as he riseth, he helps it forward, so that he both causeth it, and is caused by it. As Corruption in Doctrine, Worship, Discipline, and Manners brought him forth, so he was active in corrupting them more and more.</ns0:note>, the son of perdition <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Another <ns0:hi>Hebraism,</ns0:hi> where sometimes that which any way proceeds from another, as its cause is called its son, as sparks the sons of the coal, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 5.7. and branches sons of the tree, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49.22. and the Learner the Son of the Teacher, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3.1. and sometimes that which a man is addicted to, as a wicked man is the son of wickedness, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 89.22. Again that which gives forth what it hath in it self, as the branches of the Olive Trees giving o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>l are called the sons of Oyl, <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>ult.</ns0:hi> and in the Text, the man of sin <ns0:hi>is the Son of perdition,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> is call'd, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17.12. and he is so either actively, as he brings others to destru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction, and so may be called <ns0:hi>Apollyon, Rev.</ns0:hi> 9.11. or rather passively, as devoted to perdition; as <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 19.20. <ns0:hi>The beast and false Prophet are both cast into the lake of fire and brimstone</ns0:hi>: And the <ns0:hi>beast that was and is not,</ns0:hi> is said to go into perdition, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.11. The destroyer of others both in Soul and Body will be destroyed himself: First, Morally by the Word and Spirit, as <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 8. And then Judicially, by Gods revenging Justice in this World, and that to come. The Apostle at the very first men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioning him, declares his destiny; at his first rising and reveal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, mentions his fall and ruin.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:525" />4 Who opposeth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the Opposer, or rather opposing, exprest in the participle of the present Tense, deno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting a continued Act, or that which he bends himself strongly to: But against what? The same that he exalteth himself a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove, as some conceive, but the Grammer will not well admit that sence, and we should not so restrain it; and therefore we will take the word indefinitely, as exprest in the Text: But we may well conceive, it is Christ himself, whom he opposeth; as his Name given him by the Apostle <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> doth evidence when he is called Antichrist, or THE Antichrist, one that is against Christ; not that he openly and professedly opposeth him, but as <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> kissed his Master, and betrayed him: See those that have written of Antichrist, as <ns0:hi>Philip Nicholas, Whitaker, Danaeus Chami<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>r, Moulin, Iunius,</ns0:hi> &c. It is Iniquity in a Mistery. He serveth Christ, but it is to serve himself upon him. He ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledgeth him in all his Offices, and yet doth vertually deny and oppose him in them all; call'd Antichrist as opposite to the Unction of Christ, Christ signifies anointed, and so he opposeth him in the Offices to which he is anointed, while he owns his Natures. He professeth himself a Servant of the Servants of God, and yet persecutes, curseth, proscribes, and killeth them, opposing Christ in his Members. He maketh War with the Saints, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.7. He hath two horns like a Lamb, and speaks as a Dragon, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 11. speaks lies in Hypocrisie, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.2.</ns0:note> and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Dan. 11.36.</ns0:note> exalteth himself above all that is called God <ns0:hi>u,</ns0:hi> or that is worship<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ped: so that he, as God <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Next, he makes himself like God, and is <ns0:hi>as God,</ns0:hi> as the King of old <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> said, <ns0:hi>I will be like the most high, Isa.</ns0:hi> 14.14.</ns0:note>, sitteth in the temple of God <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">As Gods residence of old was in the Temple of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> so <ns0:hi>he sitteth as God in the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of God</ns0:hi>; not that Temple that was built by <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> and af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terwards rebuilt, and to be built again as the Popish Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctors speak: For it is now destroyed, and if it be built again by this man of sin, as they say, at his coming, would the Apostle call that the Temple of God? 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.16. <ns0:hi>Apoc.</ns0:hi> 3.12, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But it is a Spiritual Temple, as the Church is called, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.16, 17. So <ns0:hi>Aug. Hieron. Hilary, Chrysost.</ns0:hi> understand it, and he is said here to sit, to have here his Cathedra. The Apostle speaks of him as a Bishop, whose Episcopal See is called a Seat, or Cathedra, and here he sitteth as God: The Popish Writers give the Pope that, and such like Titles, <ns0:hi>Domin<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s Deus noster Papa, Idem est Dominium Dei & Papae, Tu es alter Deus in Terra. Concil. later. sess.</ns0:hi> 4. Thou art another God on Earth. And as God he maketh Laws to bind the Conscience, and dispenseth with Laws Natural and Moral, pardons sin as he pleaseth, past, present, and to come; can deliver Souls out of Purgatory, translate them to Heaven; so that this man of sin is not to be lookt for among the Turks, Pagans, or Infidels. He sitteth in the Temple, the Church of God, not that it can be the true Church, where he thus sitteth and acteth, but rather the Syna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gogue of Satan, but that which he calleth so, and which bear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth that Name, and which before the falling away, was really so, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.8. As <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> is called the Holy City after it had lost its Holiness, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 4.5. And the faithful City, when become an Harlot, and Mount <ns0:hi>Tabor</ns0:hi> an Holy Mount, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.18. be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause once so, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 1.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. or called so according to mens opini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on; as Idols that are nothing, are yet called Gods, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 28.23. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.5. Some read the words <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>in Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plum Dei,</ns0:hi> as we say, <ns0:hi>in amicum,</ns0:hi> i. e. <ns0:hi>velut amicus, He sitteth for the Temple of God,</ns0:hi> as if he himself was the Temple and Church of God. So <ns0:hi>Aug. de civ. dei.</ns0:hi> lib. 20. c. 19. And so some of our Protestant Writers applying it to the Pope, who as the Head of the Church, hath the whole Church vertually in himself, and doth exercise all Church power.</ns0:note>, shewing himself that he is God <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Not saying it with his mouth, as <ns0:hi>Oecumenius</ns0:hi> saith, but making such a shew before men. Though <ns0:hi>Bellarmin</ns0:hi> interprets it of an open boasting and vaunting himself to be God, which saith he, the Pope doth not; but by pretended Miracles, Signs, and Wonders, by Pardons, Indul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gences Canonizing Saints, Dominion over Princes and Kingdoms he shews himself as a God before men, and claiming a power to be judged of no man, and to be judge of all men. <ns0:hi>A seculari pote<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />state non solvi posse nec ligari pontificem, quem constat a</ns0:hi> Cons<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>antino <ns0:hi>Deum appellatum, cum nec Deum ab hominibus judicari manifestum sit. Decret. distinct.</ns0:hi> 96. c. 7. Yea, Lastly, he exal<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eth himself a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove God himself, when he maketh the Scriptures to derive their Authority more from the Popes Canonizing, than God himself; and without it no man is bound to believe them. <ns0:hi>Decret.</ns0:hi> lib. 2. <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 23. Again, If the Pope should err by com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manding Vice, and forbidding Vertue, the Church was bound to believe Vice to be good, and Vertue to be evil, <ns0:hi>Bellarm.</ns0:hi> lib. 4<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>de summo pont.</ns0:hi> c. 5. And it is frequent among their Divines and Canonists to say, that the Pope can dispense against the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles, and the Old Testament, and the Scriptures are inferiour to his Decrees, and without the Authority of the Church, are a Nose of Wax, Paper, and Parchment, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> so that upon the whole, as <ns0:hi>Iohns</ns0:hi> Disciples asked concerning Christ, art thou he that should come, or must we look for another; so may we not say to the Pope concerning Antichrist? Art thou he, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> I will speak boldly, either there is no Antichrist, or the Bishop of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> is he, <ns0:hi>Chamier.</ns0:hi> l. 16. c. 8.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">A further Description of this man of sin, by his Opposition and Exaltation,</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="v" place="bottom">And then he is described by his Exaltation, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, exalted, which is well supplyed, he exalteth himself. It is not from God <ns0:hi>he exalteth himself,</ns0:hi> or lifteth himself <ns0:hi>above all that is called God,</ns0:hi> though not really and essentially God. The Apostle well knew that in the Old Testament Magistrates were called Gods, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 82.1.6. and 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.5. <ns0:hi>There be that are called Gods, whether in Heaven, or in Earth.</ns0:hi> Magistrates and Rulers are of several Degrees, some Inferiour, some Superiour; some Supreme, as Kings and Emperours, but he exalteth himself above them all, and that not only in Spirituals, by Excom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />munications, but in Civils, by deposing Kings, disposing King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doms, yea, making Emperours to wait at his Ga<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e, hold his Stirrup, prostrate themselves to kiss his Toe, and then to tread upon their Neck, as <ns0:hi>Alexander</ns0:hi> the 3<ns0:hi>d.</ns0:hi> did to <ns0:hi>Frederick Barba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rossa</ns0:hi>; and this not condemned as the extravagancy of some particular persons, but allowed and justified by the Doctrine and Doctors of the <ns0:hi>Romish</ns0:hi> Church. And <ns0:hi>Bellarm. de Rom. pont.</ns0:hi> lib. 5. c. 8. gives it as the reason why the Pope would not come to the Councel of Nice, lest if the Emperour should come thither, he should attempt to sit above him; so that by these two words in the Text, the Apostle describes him both in his Enmity, and Pride, Opposition and Exaltation. Observe, First, He assumeth to himself an higher power than those that are only called Gods; theirs is Humane, his is Divine; theirs on the Bodies or Estates of men, his over the Conscience; theirs only to the Living, his to mens Souls after Death.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Remember you not, that when I was with you, I told you these things <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The Apostle tacitly upbraids them for their forgetfulness. To forget the things that have been taught us, is a great evil: <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> often cautions against it, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3.1, 4, 5. and it is often reproved, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.5. <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.24. and the contrary requi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red, <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 4.4. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 16.4. <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 17. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 3.3. <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> hid the word in his heart, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119.11. and the Virgin <ns0:hi>Mary</ns0:hi> kept the Angels saying, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.19. the Apostles did take care to tell the Churches of the Apostasie that would come, and of false Prophets and Teachers that would arise, as <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> the Elders of <ns0:hi>Ephesus, Acts</ns0:hi> 20.29, 30. and <ns0:hi>Peter,.</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.1. and <ns0:hi>St. Iohn</ns0:hi> of the coming of Antichrist, 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.18. and more fully, though obscurely in the Book of the <ns0:hi>Revelation,</ns0:hi> and the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle here in this verse minds these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> that he told them of the coming of the man of sin before the coming of Christ, so that they should not have been shaken in their minds about Christ's coming in that present Age. And they told the Chur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches of these things that they might not be surprised by them, or offended at them when they came.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And now ye know what <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>
