                        </ns0:gap>th.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> withholdeth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle it seems had told them as of his coming, so of what at present withheld the revealing of him. And what this was is difficult to know now, though it seems these <ns0:hi>Thessalo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nians</ns0:hi> knew it, there are many conjectures about it. This I shall say in general. 1. It was something that the Apostle thought not safe openly to declare in writing; else he would not have writ of it so obscurely. 2. It was both a thing, and a person, a thing, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, in this verse, that which withholdeth; and a person, as in the next verse, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, he which let<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teth, 3. It was also such a thing and such a person as were to be removed out of the way, not totally, but as they were hin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drances of this revelation. Expositors both Popish and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />testant pitch upon the Roman Emperour and Empire as most probably meant here by the Apostle. And therefore he wrote not plainly, least by writing of the taking away that Empire which the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> thought to be eternal, he might stir up their hatred against the Christians. Some understand it of the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moving only the seat of the Emperour from <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Constantino<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple,</ns0:hi> whereby the Bishop of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> had opportunity to grow up into greater power. The Popish Writers understand it of the total destruction of the Empire, which because they see not yet done they conclude the man of sin is not yet revealed. Our Protestant Writers understand it only of such a weakning of the Empire and Imperial Dominion, as gave the Bishop and Clergy of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> advantage to rise up into power both spiritual and se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular; as some learned Writers have given an account thereof. When the Empire was broken into ten Kingdoms, the Impe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rial power of the Emperours was much weakned: and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing afterwards united in the Pope as an Ecclesiastical Monarch he grew up, and the Imperial power declined, the grandeur of them both could not stand together. And this is the beast with the ten horns, and ten crowns upon the horns which is spoken of, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.1. whereupon this beast ss worshipped, and the voice ss, <ns0:hi>who is like unto the beast, who is able to make War with him? ver.</ns0:hi> 4. some of the ancient Fathers had this sense of the Text. See <ns0:hi>Tertul. l.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>de resurrect. c.</ns0:hi> 24. <ns0:hi>Chrysost. in locum. Aug. de Civ. Dei l.</ns0:hi> 19. <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 20. <ns0:hi>Ierom</ns0:hi> when he heard of the tak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Alaricus,</ns0:hi> expected the coming of <ns0:hi>Antichrist</ns0:hi> not far off. Whereupon the ancient Church did pray that the Ro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man Empire might continue long, that his coming might be de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />layed, <ns0:hi>Tertul. Apol. c.</ns0:hi> 32.39. but its now evident how it is <ns0:hi>faln</ns0:hi> from what once it was. The Eastern part is under the do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />minion of the Turk. The Western divided into ten distinct Kingdoms under distinct Government. And in <ns0:hi>Germany</ns0:hi> where it is most remaining, the Empire is little more then Titular. And <ns0:hi>Italy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> wholly in the Popes possession: and hence this man of sin hath been long since revealed.</ns0:note>, that he might be revealed in his time <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">As God ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />points seasons for all his works, so for the revealing of him, as also for his ruine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:525" />7 For the mystery of iniquity doth already work <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The way was prepared by degrees for the man of sin, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore he came actually to be revealed, or constituted in his com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pleat existence. And this was by the working of the mystery of iniquity. A mystery is something in general which is ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />struse, intricate, and not easily discerned. And there are my<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />steries in Doctrine, and in Practise; and there are mysteries of Godliness, and mysteries of iniquity, mysteries of the King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of God, and the Devils Kingdoms. So there are the deep things of God, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.10. and the depths of Satan, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2.24. the mystery ushering in the man of sin is a mystery of ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quity. It is not open sin and wickedness; but dissembled piety, specious errors, wickedness under a form of Godliness cunningly managed that is here meant. See the Book called the mystery of Jesuitisme, or the Provincial Letters. And it is a mystery that worketh; it doth exert and put forth it self, but secretly, as a Mole which worketh under ground. And its working is not against the Being, Providence, and Attributes of God, or natural Religion; but to undermine Christianity in the peculiar Doctrines, Worship, and Practise of it. In Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrines, are brought in privily damnable Heresies, 2. <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.1. In Worship, inventions and commandements of men, under pretences of greater reverence, devotion and humility, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.23. In practise, dispensations to moral impieties under colour of service to the Catholick Church. And this mystery, saith our Apostle, already worketh: in the false Doctrines of the false Teachers of his time, in the Traditions, and Inventions of men obtruding themselves into the Worship of God in his time, in the affectation of pre-eminence in the Church in his time, and making merchandise of the Gospel in his time, and gain Godliness: And in mingling Philosophical notions with the simplicity of the Gospel, and gratifying the flesh under a form of Godliness, and pretence of Gospel liberty. And it was not among the Heathen, or the Jews, but among the professours of Christianity that this mystery was then working, as I suppose the Apostle meaneth. And when the man of sin was fully re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vealed all these corruptions did centre in him, as sinks in the common shore: the lesser Antichrists in the great Antichrist.</ns0:note>, only he who now letteth <ns0:hi>will let</ns0:hi> until he be taken out of the way <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Idolatries and Persecutions of the Heathen Emperours must be taken out of the way to make way for those that arise un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der a Christian or rather Anti-christian State, the Dragon giving his Seat, Spirit, and Power to the Beast. And the Power that was in the Roman Emperour whether Heathen or Christian must be taken out of the way to make room for the Exaltation of this man of Sin. For notwithstanding all corruptions in Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine, Worship or Practise which might be introduced before, yet he is not fully revealed till he hath his jurisdiction and secu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lar power also in his hand. And then this mystery of iniquity is arrived to its height; which St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> saw written in the fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />head of the great Whore, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.5. <ns0:hi>Mystery, Babylon the great</ns0:hi> &c. and which some have said, was written anciently in the Popes Mitre.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And then shall that † wicked be revealed <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This revealing I think differs from that mentioned before <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 3. he is first revealed as I said, <ns0:hi>quoad existentiam,</ns0:hi> when he comes forth into Being, and then <ns0:hi>quoad apparentiam,</ns0:hi> when he comes to be discovered. And this I suppose is meant here, because his destruction is mentioned as following upon it. For the discovering of him is the first step to his ruine, and here is called by another name. At his first rising he is a man of sin; but after he hath violated the Laws of God, and the Laws of Christ by setting up his own, he is well called <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>that Law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less One,</ns0:hi> and now he that pretended so highly for Christ is disco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered to be Antichrist. The mystery of iniquity that before lay hid comes to be revealed, God enlightning the eyes of ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny learned Ministers and Princes, yea and of multitudes of peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple herein; the Scriptures before shut up in an unknown tongue being now translated to the understanding of the common peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, those that were made drunk with the wine of her fornica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.2. now put away their wine from them, as <ns0:hi>Eli</ns0:hi> said to <ns0:hi>Hannah.</ns0:hi> And the Kings and Kingdoms that gave their power to the beast now come to hate the whore, &c. the time being come for the fulfilling the words of God herein, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.17. And this Revelation is signified and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>oretold when the Angel said to <ns0:hi>Iohn, I will tell thee the mystery of the woman and the beast that carrieth her, Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.7. There is need of a divine Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />velation to know the mystery of iniquity, as well as the mystery of godliness. And the Woman is the same with the man of sin mentioned before, once the spouse of Christ, but now by her Idolatry becomes a whore, and divorced from him Said to be also <ns0:hi>that great City which reigneth over the Kings of the Earth,</ns0:hi> verse last; by the understanding these things this wicked one comes to be revealed.</ns0:note>; whom the Lord shall consume <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which is not done all at once; his consumption goes before his destruction. As <ns0:hi>Iezabel</ns0:hi> the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phetess who seduced the servants of God to commit Fornicati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, is said to be cast into a bed of languishing, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2.22. as he rose up by degrees so shall he be consumed gradually. His power declines by degrees both Civil and Ecclesiastical, and the authority he had got both in, and over the Consciences of men. The seven Vials are the seven last plagues which do gradually consume him; and this is said to be done by the Lord himself, which is the Lord Jesus. He that made war with the Lamb is overcome by the Lamb, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.14. Though many instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments may be imployed herein; for he is said to have those with him who are called <ns0:hi>chosen</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>faithful,</ns0:hi> ibi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and it belongs to him, as all power of Heaven and Earth is given to him, to save his people, and to destroy his adversaries; as its said of him, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 97.3. <ns0:hi>a fire goeth be<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ore him, and burneth up his ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies round about.</ns0:hi> As he is a refreshing, directing light to his people, so a consuming fire to his adversaries. The stone cut out of the mountain without hands, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 2.34. smites the image in the time of the fourth Monarchy when Christ came into the World, and in the latter end of it under the Anti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />christian state it is broken in pieces.</ns0:note> with * the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of his mouth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As was prophesied of him, <ns0:hi>Isai.</ns0:hi> 11.4. <ns0:hi>with the breath of his mouth he shall slay the wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed,</ns0:hi> even this wicked one here in the Text, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 18.8. and 19.15. And this as some interpret he shall do with ease as by a word speaking. Or by a word of command, saying, let it be done, and it shall be done. Or as we may read it, with the <ns0:hi>Spirit of his lips,</ns0:hi> because of the power or spirit that goes along with his word. But this breath of Christs mouth <ns0:hi>Ca<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>etane</ns0:hi> and others understand of the word of the Gospel, which is the breath of Christs mouth in the mouths of his Ministers, called the <ns0:hi>everlasting Gospel, Rev.</ns0:hi> 14.6. which an Angel flying through the midst of Heaven is said to have, to Preach to them that dwell upon the Earth; and then followed by another Angel, saying, <ns0:hi>Babylon is faln, is faln, verse</ns0:hi> 8. the mystery of iniquity will be unvailed by the clear preaching of the word; and the primitive pure institutions of Christ, and Doctrines of the Gospel will be vindicated from the Antichristian cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ruptions and innovations. And the spirit of Christ going forth with the Gospel will make it effectual hereunto. These <ns0:hi>are the rod of his strength whereby he rules in the midst of his Enemies, Psal.</ns0:hi> 110.2. And whereby he shall consume this man of sin. Nations and People will fall off from him as they come to understand the truth by the word Preached.</ns0:note>, and hath destroy <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">After his consuming fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lows his destruction, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the word destroy here signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies to abolish, enervate, to make of no force, and so used often in the New Testament. Sometimes applyed to the Law, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.31. somtimes to the body of sin, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.6. sometimes to persons to whom Christ will not be effectual, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.4. here to the man of sin, so that what ever remains there may be of him in the World, they shall be without any efficacy or power. His jurisdiction shall be abolish<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, his keys shall not be able to open or shut, the edge of both his Swords shall be quite blunted, his triple crown shall fall off his head, his purgatory fire shall be put out, his Images shall lose their veneration. The spell of the cross shall be detected, the intercession of Saints shall be found to be a fiction, infallibility shall be found to be a decei<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Supremacy of the Church shall fall to the ground. The rivers of his large Revenues shall be dryed up, &c. and the <ns0:hi>beast that was and is</ns0:hi> not, and <ns0:hi>yet is,</ns0:hi> shall now utterly cease to be.</ns0:note> with the brightness of his coming <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The breath of his mouth wasted him, and the brightness of his com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing destro<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>es him. Some interpret this of Christs personal coming to judgment, which will be great brightness, as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 24.27. <ns0:hi>As the lightning coming out of the East, and shineth to the West, so shall the coming of the Son of man be.</ns0:hi> Coming in the glory of Heaven, and every eye shall see him; and of this coming he spake 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 4. and in this chapter also, as that which was not so near at hand as some imagined. And without question this coming will destroy him if not destroyed before, as well as the rest of the wicked, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 1.9. but whether judgment may not first proceed against the Antichristian state, and those that have sin'd under the Gospel is a question. It is some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times mentioned particularly with respect to them. As in the parable of the Tares and Wheat, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 13. of the ten Virgins <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 25. and the Talents. And the Beast and false Prophet, are cast into the Lake of fire, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 19.20. before the Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral Judgment mentioned, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 20.12. so that at Christ's personal coming, his Judgment will as some conceive, begin here, and then proceed to the rest of the World; whereupon many assign some great length of time to Christs stay upon Earth, and judging the World. Others take the brightness of this coming in a spiritual sence, for a clearer manifestation of Christ in the World. As the Kingdom of Antichrist, or of this man of sin is founded in darkness, so the brightness of this com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing will dispel and destroy it with respect to his Eternal Generation. Christ is said to be the brightness of his Fathers Glory, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.2. but this is a brightness with respect to men. And though he hath come in his Spirit to enlighten his Church from the beginning of the World, and more eminently after his Ascension, yet this will exceed all the former, and peculi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />arly stiled the brightness of his coming: and so they expect this destruction of this man of sin before Christs coming to Judgment, for if it be the same with the fall of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned in the Revelation; many things are to be done here upon Earth after that, before Christs last coming, and they mention the calling of the Jews, the destruction of those Enemies called <ns0:hi>Gog</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Magog,</ns0:hi> the coming down of the new <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> from Heaven, which is some glorious State of the Church here upon Earth. However the Apostle here mentions nothing of a de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction by the Material Sword; what Princes may do of dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferent Religions upon a Civil account, I do not know, but as this man of sin rose out of the Apostasie of the Church, so he will not be consumed, and destroyed, but by a return from it, which is done by the <ns0:hi>breath of Christs mouth, and the brightness of his coming.</ns0:hi> But yet by some Instruments or other, God will avenge the blood of his Servants upon this man of sin in the time and way appointed of him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:526" />9 <ns0:hi>Even him</ns0:hi> who<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>e coming <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Apostle still continues his Discourse about this man of sin. He had declared whence he arose, and to what height of Power, and the manner and place of his exercising it, and what opened him the way to it, and also his destruction, with the means of it. But he thought it needful to explain particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larly the manner of his rising into all this power, and preser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving himself in it, and the persons over whom he doth exer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cise it.</ns0:note> is <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>According</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> after the working of Satan <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Christ's coming is in Power, and so is his: Christ comes with the Spirit of <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> and his is with a Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit also, but it is Satan: And the Spirit of God worketh with Christ in his coming, and the Spirit of Satan with the man of sin in his coming, which implies either the principle of this working in his coming, it is the Devil, or the similitude of it; it is like the working of Satan. If in the first sence it shews by what Spirit the Antichristian Church was first formed, and by which it is still informed and acted. As in Natural Bodies the matter is formed and informed by the Spirit within it. The true Church hath the Holy Spirit that forms it into a Spiritual Temple, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>ult.</ns0:hi> The false Church hath the Spirit of the Devil forming it into the Synagogue of Satan, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2. The Dragon is said to give the Beast his Seat, Power, and Great Authority, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.2. And this Dragon is the Devil in the Heathen Empire, who being cast out of his Seat and Power when the Emperour became Christian, found the Antichristian Church, and here exercised that Power and Authority which he did formerly in the Imperial Seat of the Heathen Empe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rours, whence we may see whence all that furious Zeal, and bloody Cruelties appearing in the Popish Church do spring, notwithstanding all their outward shews of Devotion. If we take the words in the latter sence, then his coming is like the working of Satan, either with great Power and Energy, as the word imports. The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is often used in a good sence; for Gods working in the heart, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.13. for the working of the word 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.13.                         <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Besides that Energy of Satan that works inwardly in this man of sin, which was mentioned before; he hath outward strength or power wherein he comes, which may be here meant. He hath the secular power to assist him, the Kings of the Earth giving their power to the Beast; and we read of 10 Horns upon his head, which are the Emblems of strength and power, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.1. whereupon its said; <ns0:hi>Who is like unto the Beast, who is able to make War with him,</ns0:hi> ver. 4.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 24.24.</ns0:note> signs; and lying wonders <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Some by the figure called <ns0:hi>Hendyadis</ns0:hi> read it; by the <ns0:hi>power of signs</ns0:hi> and lying wonders; but not properly. Observe how Satan is Gods Ape, God confirmed the Gospel with signs and wonders, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 25.19. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.4. <ns0:hi>God bearing them witness with signs and wonders,</ns0:hi> &c. and Satan brings this man of sin into the World in the same manner: God did it to confirm the truth, but Satan to countenance a falsehood: But though he comes with signs and wonders, yet not properly with miracles, as the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is rendred in <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2. because though the Devil can work the one, he cannot the other: He can by his great natural Knowledge and Experience improve natural causes to their utmost, but he cannot effect things above all possibility of Nature, which is the same power of Creating: The <ns0:hi>Schoolmen</ns0:hi> give their distinction between <ns0:hi>won<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ders</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>miracles,</ns0:hi> which is not needful here to insert: All mira<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cles are wonders, but all wonders are not miracles; and yet are esteemed miracles when their cause is not known. The Romish Legends are full of stories of Miracles wrought to confirm their false Doctrines of Purgatory, of Reliques, invocation of Saints, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which might be wonders really wrought by the Devil; such as were wrought by <ns0:hi>Iannes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iambres</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>Simon Magus,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Apollonius Tyaneus,</ns0:hi> &c. who used Magick Arts, and the people not knowing them in their causes, might judge them miracles. And being wrought for such ends, are termed <ns0:hi>signs</ns0:hi> for a sign is any thing that is used to make signification, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther it be a Natural, or Artificial; an Ordinary, or Extraordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary sign, used either for a good end, as those shewn by Christ, and the Apostles, or for a bad end, as those used by this man of sin. People are apt to be affected with signs. <ns0:hi>The Iews</ns0:hi> saith the Apostle, <ns0:hi>seek after a sign,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.22. as they often desired Christ to shew them a sign, and therefore this man of sin comes with signs. Some signs are only for representation, as the sign of the Cross, and the Images of Christ, and of his Death, and Resurrection, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and he comes in these: Others are for confirmation, which are either real miracles, or such as seem so; and he comes in these latter also, which are here cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>lying wonders;</ns0:hi> or wonders of a lye, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Though the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word is oft used for a real miracle, yet nor so here; for miracles are the effects of a Divine Power only, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.19. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.4. and not Diabolical. And call'd <ns0:hi>lying wonders,</ns0:hi> either because they are used to confirm a lye, or be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they are not real, but fained wonders; Impostors to cheat the people, and make them wonder; whereof we have account in <ns0:hi>Gregories</ns0:hi> Dialogues, and in <ns0:hi>Paulus Diaconus,</ns0:hi> and o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers, and yet such miracles are these the Papists boast of as marks of their Church to be true, though they are here by the Apostle made the marks of the man of sin. And Christ fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tels of false Prophets that should shew <ns0:hi>great signs,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>wonders,</ns0:hi> to deceive, if possible, the very Elect. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 24.24. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13.1. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.13, 14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And with all deceivableness of unrighteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or deceit of unrighteousness, unrighteous deceit, or deceit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful unrighteousness. And it is universal, <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi>; It is unrighte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness managed with great subtilty to deceive: And so the same with the mystery of iniquity mentioned before, or the mystery of unrighteousness, as we may read it. All sin is unrighteousness, whether against God or man, as all vertue is comprehended in righteousness. The Apostle here means unrighteousness so cloaked and covered, that men discer<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> it not, but are deceived by it. As the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> who devoured Wi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dows houses, and for pretence made long Prayers. And so also they tithed Mint and Cummin as exactly religious, built the Sepulchres of the Prophets, made broad their Philacte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries, would not eat with unwashen hands, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> The like we find in the Church of <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> as I mentioned before, where men are ambitious, covetous, cruel, superstitious, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and all under a pretence of righteousness, and for honour to Christ, and the Church. Make use of <ns0:hi>Peters</ns0:hi> keys to open rich mens Coffers; and for a sum of money to absolve men in this world, or to redeem them out of Purgatory in the other World; which is a meer cheat, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Thus comes this man of sin, and by such waies he hath advanced himself.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 2.15. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 4.3.</ns0:note> them <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> that perish <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This shews who they are that are deceived by him. Reprobates are often so described, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.15. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.3. and it is the same as else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where signifies damnation. The word signifies men that are lost, so used <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 18.11. or destroyed, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.9. They are such as have not their Names written in the Book of Life, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 13.8. And who shall drink of the Wine of the Wrath of God, and the smoke of their torment ascendeth for ever, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 14, 10, 11.</ns0:note>, because they received not the love of the truth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And the Apostle gives the reason why they are thus deceived. He saith not, they had not received the Truth, but the love of it, and so hold it not fast, but are carryed away with the general Apostasie; Truth is either Natural, which the Heathen had, and detain'd in unrighteousness, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.18. or supernatural from Divine Revelation. This is meant, for he speaks not of Heathens, but Christians, not the World, but the Church.</ns0:note> that they might be saved <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And the truth here meant is saving Truth, as the Gospel is called the word of Truth, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.13. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.5. for had they received it in Love, they <ns0:hi>might have been saved</ns0:hi>; but for want of that they perish; so that it is unsound notional profes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sours that are carryed away by the man of sin, and deceived by him. Truth, if it be not received into the heart as well as the head, it will not secure against Apostasie, or Popery, nor prevent perishing. And the amiableness that is in Gospel. Truths calls for Love, as the certainty of its Revelation calls for Faith, and had they so received the Truth, they might have been saved.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And for this cause God shall send them ‖ strong delusions <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">We had account in the former verse of such as are deceiv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by the man of sin, of their sin, and here of their punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment. They were first deluded, which was their sin, and God sends them strong delusion and that is their punishment. They did not receive the Truth in the love of it, which was their sin, and therefore are given up to believe a lye, which is their pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishment. Had they received the Truth aright, they might have been saved, but not receiving it they are damned. And they were said to be such as perish, and their perishing is here call'd damnation. So that though God is not the Authour of sin, or falshood, <ns0:hi>Deus non est author cujus est ultor.</ns0:hi> Fulgent. Yet he may in Justice give men up to them, which the Apostle here calls Gods sending, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which imports either, 1. Tradition, deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vering men to Satan to tempt, and deceive. 2. Desertion, with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />holding, or withdrawing that grace that might preserve them. 3. A judicial permission, God purposing not to hinder men to fall into that sin or delusions which he seeth their own hearts incline them to. God concurs to evil, not <ns0:hi>positive,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>priva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tive</ns0:hi>; not <ns0:hi>efficienter,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>deficienter; Schoolmen.</ns0:hi> God in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture is often said to do that which he permits to be done, as in the case of <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> selling into <ns0:hi>Egypt, Gen.</ns0:hi> 45.7. <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s numbring the People, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 24.1. compar'd with 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 21.1. And the ten Kings giving their power to the Beast, by Gods putting it into their hearts, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.17. and it is not a bare permission, for what evil God permits, he decreed to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mit it; and he decreed the circumstances attending it, and the end to which he would order and dispose it. And the degree to which it should break forth. They were deceived into error, and God gave them up to it. And it did work with great effi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cacy. Which either relates to the man of sin that did lead them strongly into it, or to them that were led by him, when error doth vitiate the life, and one error begets another, and makes men violent against the truth, then it is the efficacy of error. And thus God doth judicially punish sin with sin, and delusion with delusion. And then they are alwayes most ope<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rative, and most incurable. But men fall not presently under these judicial acts; men first refuse to see before God sends blindness, and first harden their own hearts before God har<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dens them. These in the Text first refused to receive the Truth before they were given up to believe a lye; see <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.24. so that both God, and this man of sin, and themselves also are concerned in these evils; but they sinfully and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />righteously, but God judicially and in Righteousness.</ns0:note>, that they should believe as lye <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And the Lye they were given up to believe, is a Doctrinal Lye; false speaking is a lye in words, Hypocrisie is a lye in fact, and Error is a lye in Doctrine. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 11.12. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 5.3. Some by Lye, here suppose is meant the lying wonders before mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed; and this sence need not be excluded, but I rather mean it of false Doctrine, as that which stands opposite to the Truth before mentioned, and again mentioned in this verse. Some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times Idols are called lies, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 44.20. sometimes the things of the World; <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 4.2. sometimes the great men of the World, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 62.9. sometimes false Divinations, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 22.28. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 10.2. sometimes false prophesyings and predictions, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 14.14, 23, 25, 26. and sometimes false Doctrines, as 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.2. where we read of false prophets, who shall arise in the last time, and <ns0:hi>speak lies in hypocrisie, &c.</ns0:hi> and false Apostles are said to be Liars upon that account, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2.2. And such are many <ns0:hi>Popish</ns0:hi> Doctrines which the Apostle here probably refers to. What is Transubstantiation but a lye; Purgatory, Infallibility of the Church, Mediation of Saints, their <ns0:hi>opus operatum, &c.</ns0:hi> Men must be strongly deluded to believe such Doctrines, and it is mentioned as a great Judgment of God upon them to believe such lies, as it is a great Mercy to believe the Truth, especially if we consider what follows upon it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:526" />12 That they all might be <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>judged.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> damned <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>That they all might be damned,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>condemned.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> is <ns0:hi>judged,</ns0:hi> but often translated as in the Text; the simple Verb being taken for the compound; so <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3.17. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.29. <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 4. Its true a man may be judged and not condemned, but the judgment of the wicked is condemnation; and damnation is here mentioned either as the event, or the effect of their be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieving Lies, or as the purpose of God in sending them strong delusions. They are first justly punish'd with spiritual judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, and then eternal, and God is just in both, whence we see that there are some Errors in judgment which are damna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble. As we read 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.1. <ns0:hi>of damnable heresies,</ns0:hi> or heresies of destruction; such are many in the <ns0:hi>Romish</ns0:hi> Church; and the Apostle speaks of such, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.19. <ns0:hi>not holding the head, &c.</ns0:hi> not meant of a total rejection of Christ, but of voluntary Hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mility, and worshipping of Angels mingled with the true Wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship of the Gospel; and such cannot be saved.</ns0:note>, who believed not the truth <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Where we have a farther description of these Persons who are to be dam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned, which is added by the Apostle either to clear Gods Justice, as in sending them strong delusions to believe a lye, so also in their condemnation, or to assign the cause why they believed a lye, is because they believed not the Truth. Those will easily be brought to believe a lye, who believe not the Truth; and the belief here mentioned is that of assent, yet such an assent as is operative and practical, which they had not; for it was said before, <ns0:hi>they received not the Truth in the love of it.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.<ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">2. <ns0:hi>Because they had pleasure in unrighteousness.</ns0:hi> Did not only practise, but had great complacence and contentment of mind in it, as the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> word imports, and so had rather believe a false doctrine, which will countenance their practise, than the Truth which doth condemn it. See <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10.23. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>last.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />righteousness,</ns0:hi> some Expositions understand <ns0:hi>false Doctrine,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Error,</ns0:hi> because it is set in opposition here to Truth, as sin is set in op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />position to it, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8.45. and that the Apostle hath peculiar reference to the corrupt Doctrines of <ns0:hi>Simon Magus</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Ni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />colaitans,</ns0:hi> that gave liberty to the Lusts of the Flesh. But why not rather to the Doctrines of the <ns0:hi>Man of Sin,</ns0:hi> which he had been before speaking of? I rather take the word in the largest sence, so all sin in unrighteousness; and the Apostle St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>all unrighteousness is sin,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 5.17, where unrighte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness is exprest by <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> a word which imports transgressi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of the Law, as in this Text by <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, a word which sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies injustice. So that we see here an erroneous Mind, and a vicious life going together. And when sin is come to this height, that men take pleasure in it, it makes them ripe for damnation. And how well these things agree to the Antichri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian Church, let men consider and judge.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The Apostle here exempts these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> out of the number of those Reprobates, that he had before spoken of, and speaks of them as such as should be preserved from Apostasie in Faith or Practise, and obtain Salvation. And this he men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions for comfort to them, and with thanksgivings to God. He had often before given thanks for them, 1 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 1.2. and 2.13. and 3.9. and in the former Chapter of this Epistle <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 3. and both here and there mentions it as a debt he was bound unto, or a duty he owed, we ought to give thanks, as in the <ns0:hi>Greek.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, brethren, beloved of the Lord <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And here he stiles them, not only brethren, as often before, but <ns0:hi>beloved of the Lord</ns0:hi>; such as have been, and are be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loved. And therefore not in the number of them that should be damned, mentioned in the former verse.</ns0:note>, because God hath from the beginning ‖ chosen you to salvation <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which words are either to give the reason of the Apostles Thanksgivings; or rather all Arguments to evidence they were beloved of the Lord. And he instanceth in their Election as a proof of it. There is an Election of Office, as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to the King, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6.21. and <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> to be an Apostle, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6.70. and Election to a visible Church, and means of Salvation; and thus the seed of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> were chosen, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 26.18. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 135.4. & 147.19, 20. and Election to Salvation, as in the Text; which is either that which follows Faith, as some understand that place, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 22.14. or rather that which goes before it; said here to be <ns0:hi>from the beginning</ns0:hi>; not from the beginning of the Gospel as some say; nor from the beginning of our Preaching to you, or of your effectual Calling, as others say; no nor yet is it meant from the beginning of the World, which was the beginning of the time; or immediately upon <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi>'s Fall; but by beginning is here meant Eternity it self, as Election, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.4. is said to be from before the foundation of the World, which is from Eter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity. Though <ns0:hi>beginning</ns0:hi> seems to relate to time, yet the Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures often express Eternity by such words as relate to time. As when God is called <ns0:hi>the Ancient of dayes, Dan.</ns0:hi> 7.9. it signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies his Eternity; and <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> speaks of some that were of old or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dained to condemnation, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Gods Eter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal decrees being compared to a book wherein names are written, <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 4. when was their ordaining but from Eternity? and it is Election to Salvation, compleat Salvation, which is here meant, in the full fruition of it; not in the Title to it by Faith, or the first fruits of it in Sanctification, because they are here mentioned as the means that tend to it.</ns0:note>, through sanctification of the Spirit <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Election is to the means as well as the end, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.4. Holiness is not the cause of Gods Election, but God hath decreed it to be the way to Salvation; <ns0:hi>without holiness none shall ever set the Lord, Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.14.</ns0:note>, and belief of the Truth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">And therefore those were spoken of as persons to be damned, who believed not the Truth in the former verse. And so its evident, Election is not upon the foresight of Faith, it is through it we have Salvation, but not Election: But of this before, 1 <ns0:hi>Epist.</ns0:hi> 4. And the Apostle joyns Sanctification and Faith together for they are not and cannot be put together. Now by all this the Apostle proves they were beloved of the Lord. He saw the fruits of Election in their Sanctification and belief of the Truth, thence concludes they were Elected, and therefore loved.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Whereunto ‖ he called you by our gospel <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Before, the Apostle mentioned their Election, now their Calling; and are often in Scripture put together, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.30. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.10. and are both applyed to Christ himself, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 42.1.6. They are those two Soveraign Acts of God, pre-requisit to a State of Salvation. The one Eternal, the other in time; the one immanent in God, the other tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sient upon the Creature, and it is the first transient Act that flows from Election. And because there is an outward and inward Call mentioned in Scripture, we must here understand the Apostle of both: For <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>whereunto, or to which thing,</ns0:hi> mentioned in the beginning of this verse, refers to all that he said in the former verse, which is, Salvation, Sanctification, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lief of the Truth, which they could not attain with a meer out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward call; though they had that also: For the Apostle menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons here the Gospel, which he calls <ns0:hi>our Gospel,</ns0:hi> because preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by them, and intrusted to them, though the Original of it is from God, and the matter of it from Jesus Christ: And he puts them in mind of the great mercy they had received in their Preaching the Gospel to them, for thereby they were called in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to a state of Salvation; As also of the way wherein they are to obtain tis Salvation, which is through Sanctification of the Spirit, and the belief of the Truth, that they might be careful to persevere both in Faith and Holiness; and not to expect it from the Law; or the speculations of Philosophy, which some false Teachers might suggest, for as Faith comes by hearing the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.17. so it is that only which is the power of God to salvation, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.16. And by this he confirms to them also their Election, because they had been thus effectually called by the Gospel: For no man can conclude his Salvation from Election, if he hath not been also thus called, which is by feeling the power of the Gospel in the heart, and yielding obe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dience to it in his Life.</ns0:note>, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">What the Apostle before call'd Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation, he here stiles the <ns0:hi>obtaining the Glory of our Lord Iesus Christ. A.</ns0:hi> Though in the 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.9. he had there also cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led it obtaining Salvation, and by the same word here used in the Text: Yea the word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> here rendred <ns0:hi>obtaining,</ns0:hi> sometimes signifies Salvation it self, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:hi>last.</ns0:hi> and which is equivalent, <ns0:hi>the purchased possession, Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.14. and it may signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fie in the Text, the obtaining the glory of Christ in a way of purchase, as also by diligent endeavours after it, by way of ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quisition, as the word seems to signifie. And by the glory of Christ is not meant the glory we give to him, as some would strain the words to that sence, but rather the glory we shall re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive from him, which is the same which the Father hath given to him, and which he hath given to his people. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 17.22. whereby they are co-heirs with him, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.17. And so the Apostle sets forth the greatness of this Salvation, to which these Believers were called, it is to the obtaining the same glory with Christ, in kind at least; and shews their different state from those that perish, and will be damned, mentioned in the former verses, Or if we read the words, <ns0:hi>ye are called to be</ns0:hi> a peculiar people, as the Greek word is so rendered, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.9. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> a peculiar people. And understand by the glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry of Christ, that glory of his grace he hath manifested herein, it shews also how God hath distinguisht them from those before mentioned.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:527" />15 Therefore, brethren, stand fast <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The former verses contained Consolation, this is an Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hortation: The Apostle had assured them of their being elected and called, yet exhorts them to their duty. Assurance of sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation doth not encourage negligence, the Apostle takes his Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument from thence to quicken them, <ns0:hi>Therefore, &c.</ns0:hi> And that which he exhorts them to, is, 1. To stand fast, a Military word, speaking as a Captain to his Souldiers, so 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.13. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.14. having before foretold a great Apostasie that would come: Or because he had told them of the great glory they had been called to the obtaining of by the Gospel; He exhorts them to stand fast, which implies a firm perswasion of mind, and constant purpose of will; and stands opposite to hesitation, and despondency. 2. <ns0:hi>To hold the Traditions which they had been taught.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>hold with strength.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> hold the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 3.6.</ns0:note> traditions which ye have been taught <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The word <ns0:hi>Tradition</ns0:hi> signifies any thing delivered to another; especially meant of Doctrines. The Pharisees Doctrine is called Traditions, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.3. And so the true Doctrines of the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel, being such as the Apostles delivered to the people: as the Doctrine of the Lords Supper is said to be delivered, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.23. and so <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 6.13.</ns0:note>, whether by word or our epistle <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By word of mouth in publick preaching, or private instruction. The Apostle had both preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and written to these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians,</ns0:hi> before he wrote this se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond Epistle. And that the Papists should hence infer that there are matters of necessary consequence in Religion, not con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tained in the Scriptures is without ground: These they call Traditions, some whereof are concerning Faith, others con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning manners, others ritual, with respect to the worship of God, or the external polity of the Church. But who can as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure us what these are? what a dore is here opened to intro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duce what men please into the Church, under pretence of Tra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dition? who were the persons the Aopstle intrusted to keep these Traditions? why should he not declare the whole system of Gospel truths he had received from Christ in writing, as well as part? why should he conceal some things, when he wrote others? And doth not the Apostle assure <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>all Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture is by inspiration of God, and is profitable for Doctrine, for re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proof, for correction, for instruction, that the man of God may be per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect, throughly furnished unto all good works,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.16, 17. What need then Traditions? And how can we know that they are by Divine inspiration, as we are assured all Scripture is. Our Saviour reproved the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> about their Traditions, when from hence they would observe and impose Ceremonies of wash<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing hands, Cups and Platters, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.2. yea, and by them make the Commandments of God of none effect, which the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle cautions the <ns0:hi>Colossians</ns0:hi> about, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.8. and whereof <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> declares his zeal before his Conversion, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.14. and we find mens zeal still more about them then Moral duties, and express Institutions of Gods Worship. All the Apostles Doctrine, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther by word or Epistle, he calls by the name of Tradition, in the Text here, and he commends the <ns0:hi>Corinthians,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11.2. <ns0:hi>That they kept the Traditions delivered to them</ns0:hi>; But were not they all committed to writing in some place or other of his Epistles, and which were, and which were not, who can be certain? And why should <ns0:hi>Traditions</ns0:hi> be confined only to those things which the Apostle did not write? He exhorts the <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> to hold the Traditions which they had been taught, <ns0:hi>whether by word or Epistle.</ns0:hi> And if they hold them with strength, as the word is, by this means they would stand fast.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Now <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Apostle here addeth Prayer to his Exhortation, the word and prayer are to go together, whether it be written or preached; as he told the Disciples, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 6.4. <ns0:hi>We will give our selves to the World and Prayer.</ns0:hi> He had planted them a Church, but he knew God gives the encrease, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.6.</ns0:note> our Lord Jesus Christ himself <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons he prayes to are here, first, our Lord Jesus Christ, which was a good Argument in <ns0:hi>Athanasius</ns0:hi>'s his time, for the dignity of Christ, against the <ns0:hi>Arrians,</ns0:hi> and so it is still, and now against the <ns0:hi>Socinians</ns0:hi>: For God alone is the object of worship, and the bestower of those gifts which he here prayes for. Only the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle when he mentions Christ delights to mention him in his relation to his people, so he doth for the most part in all his Epistles, and so in this Text. He useth a Pronoun Possessive, <ns0:hi>our,</ns0:hi> for it is relation and interest which commendeth and sweet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neth any good to us.</ns0:note>, and God even our father <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And the other person is God the Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, who is the Father of Lights, from whom cometh every good and perfect gift, <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 1.17. and whom in his prayer he mentions, together with Christ; because no access can be to God, but through Christ, and no good gift descends to us, but through him. And so God the Father is mentioned in his rela<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to his people also, <ns0:hi>God even our Father</ns0:hi>; and when Christ is ours, in him God is ours also. And the Apostle thus looking, and thus speaking of Christ, and of God, strengthens his own, and their Faith, for the obtaining of the gifts he prayes for.</ns0:note>, which hath loved us <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Another Argument is from Gods love; our doubts in prayer arise more from unbelief in Gods will, then his power, which will vanish when we look upon him in his love to us; for the nature of love is <ns0:hi>velle bonum,</ns0:hi> to will good to whom we love.</ns0:note>, and given <ns0:hi>us</ns0:hi> everlasting consolation <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Another is, from gifts already received, which are first <ns0:hi>ever<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lasting Consolation,</ns0:hi> whereby it appears, that Gods love is commu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nicative, and that it is not common, but his special love he spake of. Outward comforts are common gifts, but these the Apostle means not here, because they are not everlasting; they continue not beyond death; they begin in time and end with time, but this Consolation begins in time; and abides to Eter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity, and this man cannot give, the world cannot give, nor we give it our selves, God giveth it only; and he gives it to whom he loveth. As every man seeks to comfort those whom he loves and though some whom God loves may not feel his consolation, yet they have a right, and God hath it in reserve for them. <ns0:hi>Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart, Psal.</ns0:hi> 97.11. And though sometimes it may be interrupted where it is felt, yet not so as to be destroy'd in its foundation, and to hinder its return, either in the Temporal or Eternal World, where it will be everlasting; so that as God is stiled <ns0:hi>the God of all grace,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> 5.10. <ns0:hi>So the God of all comfort,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> 1.3. And by <ns0:hi>us</ns0:hi> in the Text he means these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> as well as himself, for he had spoken before of their joy in the Holy Ghost, 1 <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> 1.6.</ns0:note>, and good hope <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And the other gift is, <ns0:hi>good hope.</ns0:hi> Hope as a natural affection is the expectation of the Soul; and the object of it is <ns0:hi>bonum futurum, arduum, p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ssibiie</ns0:hi>; Good, future good, difficult, and possible. But as a Grace, so it is the expectation of the good things God hath promised, and not yet exhibited. And its call'd good hope, good by way of eminency, with respect to the objects of it, which are eminently good. The certainty of it, it will not make ashamed, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.5. compar'd to an Anchor sure and stedfast, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.19. The regularness of it; things promis'd only, and as they are promised; else it is presump<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion and not hope. The fruits of it; Peace, Purity, Industry, and Consolation also, and therefore joyned with it here in the Text: as the Apostle speaks else-where of <ns0:hi>rejoycing in hope, Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.2. & 12.12. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 3.6. Or, as some, is called good hope, with respect to the degree they had attained of it in their hearts. Though they had not yet the good things promised, yet they had good hope of enjoying them. And by this Epi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thet he distinguisheth this hope from the carnal vain hope of the men of the World, and the false hope of Hypocrites, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 8.13.17.18. and themselves also from the state they were in when <ns0:hi>Gentiles; without hope, Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.12. and this also is Gods gift, as he is called <ns0:hi>the God of hope, Rom.</ns0:hi> 15.13. not only as the object, but the Author of it.</ns0:note>, through grace <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And both these gifts are said to be here, <ns0:hi>through Grace</ns0:hi>; for else we could have had no ground either of hope, or comfort. Sin had shut up our way to both, it is only Grace that hath opened it to us. What we enjoy at present, and what we hope to enjoy is all through Grace. And from these gifts already received the Apostle strengthens his Faith about the other things he here prays for.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 Comfort your hearts <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Next, we have the things pray'd for, <ns0:hi>Comfort your hearts</ns0:hi> Though he said before, <ns0:hi>who hath given us everlasting consolation.</ns0:hi> Either the Apostle means, actual possession of what God had given Title to; or a continued supply and encrease of comfort already received. And he prays for this either in respect of the afflictions they suffered, that they might not faint; or to enable them the better to stand fast in the Faith, and not fall away as others. And so it agrees with the next Petition for them.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Thes. 3.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> stablish you in every good word and work <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The word of Truth is this good word, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 4.2. as the Gospel is call'd, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.7. And the Doctrines of it are all good, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.6. They are good <ns0:hi>for instruction, for correction, for reproof, for doctrine,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.16. All truth is an intel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lectual good, whether natural, or moral; but evangelical Truth is by way of eminence, good: It is a good word which is a word of Salvation, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.26. and to be establish'd in it, is firmly to believe it, and to hold it fast against seducing opinion, or persecutions; and by every good word he means all Divine Truth especially the greater Truths; not to hold some Truths and let others goe. And to <ns0:hi>word</ns0:hi> the Apostle adds work, that there may be an harmony betwixt Faith and Practise. As the Doctrine of the Gospel are true, so the works they require are good. And good works are manifold, respecting God, our Neighbour, and our selves. A Christian should not only prac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tise them all, but be establish'd in them, which implyes con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stancy, perseverance and resolution. True Religion is not word only, but work; it is not only speculative, but practical. A sound Mind ought to be joyn'd with an holy Life. And to make a work good, the principle, rule, manner and end must all be good.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
